item.title: ‘Our Culture’: Deaf Nigerians Embrace Indigenous Sign Languages
item.description: With a quick flick of the wrist, Umaru Zayyanu conveys the phrase “I am a Nigerian”. But the 37-year-old is not speaking — or signing, rather — in the official sign language, Nigerian Sign Language (NSL). Instead, he’s using Hausa sign language. Such indigenous sign languages abound in the country, where deaf people were communicating with each other long before the advent of formal sign language taught in deaf schools, in 1960. Today, Nigeria, like many countries on the continent with limited education budgets, has a hard enough time placing children in dedicated schools for the deaf and hard of hearing. And there’s even less attention paid to local sign languages used outside the school system — a serious disservice to the country’s linguistic diversity, Festus Zenda, who has worked on documentation projects with local deaf communities, told AFP. “These indigenous signing systems should be studied, documented and preserved before changes in education, migration, technology and wider use of Nigerian Sign Language cause some of them to decline or disappear,” said Zenda, who has helped document the local sign language used by the Tiv ethnic group, in Benue state. A deaf resident gestures with his fingers while conversing during a community meeting in Zuba, near Abuja, on October 16, 2026. (Photo by LIGHT ORIYE TAMUNOTONYE / AFP) Sani Lawali (3R), a deaf resident gestures with his hands while conversing during a community meeting in Zuba, near Abuja, on October 16, 2026. (Photo by LIGHT ORIYE TAMUNOTONYE / AFP) Festus Zenda, Deaf Advocate and Indigenous Sign Language Promoter, with Nigeria’s National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), uses sign language to converse during a video call along a street in Abuja, on October 16, 2026. (Photo by LIGHT ORIYE TAMUNOTONYE / AFP) Displacement by formal signing The working-class Abuja exurb of Zuba is a symphony of motorcycle horns, plantain hawkers’ shouts and the dull hum of construction work. Another group adds their own, milder contributions: claps, muffled shouts of exclamation and the swish of rapid hand gestures as they chat in Hausa signs. Nigerian sign languages, like their spoken counterparts, are sometimes confined to a small number of speakers in a country crowded with some 500 tongues and an unknown number of sign languages. But Hausa sign language has become a lingua franca for deaf people across the north of the country. “I cherish my culture, I cherish my indigenous sign language,” Sanni Lawal, who runs a laundry business in Zuba’s crowded market, told AFP through an interpreter. “I want it to expand everywhere.” Nigeria traces its official sign language to Andrew Foster, an American who introduced formal deaf education across a swathe of African countries at the dawn of independence from colonial powers. Many countries in the region today use an official sign language based on American Sign Language. But in the decades since, some scholars argue indigenous signing
item.dc:creator: Nebianet Usaini
item.content:encoded: With a quick flick of the wrist, Umaru Zayyanu conveys the phrase “I am a Nigerian”. But the 37-year-old is not speaking — or signing, rather — in the official sign language, Nigerian Sign Language (NSL). Instead, he’s using Hausa sign language. Such indigenous sign languages abound in the country, where deaf people were communicating with each other long before the advent of formal sign language taught in deaf schools, in 1960. Today, Nigeria, like many countries on the continent with limited education budgets, has a hard enough time placing children in dedicated schools for the deaf and hard of hearing. And there’s even less attention paid to local sign languages used outside the school system — a serious disservice to the country’s linguistic diversity, Festus Zenda, who has worked on documentation projects with local deaf communities, told AFP. “These indigenous signing systems should be studied, documented and preserved before changes in education, migration, technology and wider use of Nigerian Sign Language cause some of them to decline or disappear,” said Zenda, who has helped document the local sign language used by the Tiv ethnic group, in Benue state. A deaf resident gestures with his fingers while conversing during a community meeting in Zuba, near Abuja, on October 16, 2026. (Photo by LIGHT ORIYE TAMUNOTONYE / AFP) Sani Lawali (3R), a deaf resident gestures with his hands while conversing during a community meeting in Zuba, near Abuja, on October 16, 2026. (Photo by LIGHT ORIYE TAMUNOTONYE / AFP) Festus Zenda, Deaf Advocate and Indigenous Sign Language Promoter, with Nigeria’s National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), uses sign language to converse during a video call along a street in Abuja, on October 16, 2026. (Photo by LIGHT ORIYE TAMUNOTONYE / AFP) Displacement by formal signing The working-class Abuja exurb of Zuba is a symphony of motorcycle horns, plantain hawkers’ shouts and the dull hum of construction work. Another group adds their own, milder contributions: claps, muffled shouts of exclamation and the swish of rapid hand gestures as they chat in Hausa signs. Nigerian sign languages, like their spoken counterparts, are sometimes confined to a small number of speakers in a country crowded with some 500 tongues and an unknown number of sign languages. But Hausa sign language has become a lingua franca for deaf people across the north of the country. “I cherish my culture, I cherish my indigenous sign language,” Sanni Lawal, who runs a laundry business in Zuba’s crowded market, told AFP through an interpreter. “I want it to expand everywhere.” Nigeria traces its official sign language to Andrew Foster, an American who introduced formal deaf education across a swathe of African countries at the dawn of independence from colonial powers. Many countries in the region today use an official sign language based on American Sign Language. But in the decades since, some scholars argue indigenous signing has languished as governments have prioritised formal languages. “People gather in the moonlight narrating their folklores in indigenous sign,” said Joshua Gyang, who has researched local languages with Nigeria’s deaf activist community. Nevertheless, he warned they will “certainly perish” without preservation. Deaf residents use sign language to converse during a community meeting in Zuba, near Abuja, on October 16, 2026. (Photo by LIGHT ORIYE TAMUNOTONYE / AFP) ‘Our culture and identity’ The government doesn’t completely ignore local sign languages: politicians often bring Hausa signers to campaign stops to court deaf voters, Zuba residents told AFP. The strategy makes sense: there’s no school there to teach formal sign language. Under a USAID programme administered by Gallaudet University — the United States’ premier university for deaf and hard of hearing students, and Foster’s alma mater — researchers were providing training to deaf educators in Nigeria, which touched on local languages as well. In a 2024 update, the university said their work sparked discussions around languages like Hausa sign language and whether they “deserve recognition and should be the medium of instruction in schools”. The programme was shut down last year as Washington slashed foreign aid spending. Nevertheless, Nigerian researchers and activists like Zenda, Zayyanu, Gyang and their colleague Taiwo Ajayi continue to document indigenous sign languages. Even Nigerian sign language has its own local flair, Ajayi, a sign language interpreter, told AFP, noting the differences in the way signs are taught in school and the way people actually converse in the street. For Hausa signers, their language has become a key part of “our culture and identity”, Zayyanu told AFP. “Even before we go to school, we have our own language,” he said. “Instead of burying that one, why not develop it?” The post ‘Our Culture’: Deaf Nigerians Embrace Indigenous Sign Languages appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: 2027: Reset your mind, align with people’s choice, Oshiomhole tells Makinde
item.description: By Adeola Badru Senator Adams Oshiomhole, former Governor of Edo State, has urged Oyo State Governor and presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Seyi Makinde, to reconsider his political position ahead of the 2027 general elections, saying the country needed leaders committed to sustaining progress. Oshiomhole, who spoke in Ibadan on Saturday during President Bola Tinubu’s rally at the historic Mapo Hall, challenged Makinde to align himself with the wishes of the electorate, insisting that the governor must first reconsider his own position on Tinubu’s re-election bid. The former Edo governor, who expressed support for Tinubu’s second-term ambition, described the forthcoming election as a decisive moment for Nigeria and questioned whether Makinde’s call for a reset was intended to reverse policies he said had benefited ordinary Nigerians. “This coming election is a decisive factor. We have a leader, the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu,” he said. Oshiomhole said he had questions for Makinde over his position on Tinubu’s continuation in office, particularly regarding the administration’s student loan scheme, infrastructure development, and improved welfare for university lecturers. He asked whether Makinde’s opposition to the president’s re-election was connected to the federal government’s decision to provide financial assistance to students from poor backgrounds through the student loan scheme. “Is Seyi Makinde angry because Tinubu is giving loans to the children of poor people in our universities? Is that what Makinde wants to reset?” he asked. The senator also questioned whether the governor intended to reverse the federal government’s infrastructure projects, particularly the coastal highway linking Lagos to Calabar, which he said would improve connectivity and make movement easier for Nigerians. “The President is creating massive infrastructure to connect Lagos to Calabar so that our people can move. Is that what Makinde wants to reset?” he said. Oshiomhole further challenged Makinde’s position on the welfare of university lecturers, citing the University of Ibadan as an example of an institution that had previously experienced repeated disruptions to its academic calendar due to industrial action. He recalled that university lecturers had, in the past, frequently embarked on strikes, disrupting academic activities and delaying students’ graduation. “For this city has the most outstanding university in Africa, the University of Ibadan. For a long, long time, the lecturer will teach you for two days and then will go on strike for three days. Is that not true?” he said. item.dc:creator: Ayobami
item.content:encoded: By Adeola Badru Senator Adams Oshiomhole, former Governor of Edo State, has urged Oyo State Governor and presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Seyi Makinde, to reconsider his political position ahead of the 2027 general elections, saying the country needed leaders committed to sustaining progress. Oshiomhole, who spoke in Ibadan on Saturday during President Bola Tinubu’s rally at the historic Mapo Hall, challenged Makinde to align himself with the wishes of the electorate, insisting that the governor must first reconsider his own position on Tinubu’s re-election bid. The former Edo governor, who expressed support for Tinubu’s second-term ambition, described the forthcoming election as a decisive moment for Nigeria and questioned whether Makinde’s call for a reset was intended to reverse policies he said had benefited ordinary Nigerians. “This coming election is a decisive factor. We have a leader, the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu,” he said. Oshiomhole said he had questions for Makinde over his position on Tinubu’s continuation in office, particularly regarding the administration’s student loan scheme, infrastructure development, and improved welfare for university lecturers. He asked whether Makinde’s opposition to the president’s re-election was connected to the federal government’s decision to provide financial assistance to students from poor backgrounds through the student loan scheme. “Is Seyi Makinde angry because Tinubu is giving loans to the children of poor people in our universities? Is that what Makinde wants to reset?” he asked. The senator also questioned whether the governor intended to reverse the federal government’s infrastructure projects, particularly the coastal highway linking Lagos to Calabar, which he said would improve connectivity and make movement easier for Nigerians. “The President is creating massive infrastructure to connect Lagos to Calabar so that our people can move. Is that what Makinde wants to reset?” he said. Oshiomhole further challenged Makinde’s position on the welfare of university lecturers, citing the University of Ibadan as an example of an institution that had previously experienced repeated disruptions to its academic calendar due to industrial action. He recalled that university lecturers had, in the past, frequently embarked on strikes, disrupting academic activities and delaying students’ graduation. “For this city has the most outstanding university in Africa, the University of Ibadan. For a long, long time, the lecturer will teach you for two days and then will go on strike for three days. Is that not true?” he said. The former governor said the Tinubu administration had deliberately prioritized the welfare of university lecturers, whom he described as critical to developing the country’s future workforce. He argued that improved remuneration for lecturers would strengthen the education sector, encourage qualified academics to remain in the profession, and ensure that students could complete their studies without repeated interruptions. “I just want to deliver this message. Now, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has deliberately decided that those who make the manpower of tomorrow are the lecturers in our universities.” “And he has increased their pay substantially so that for four years, your academic calendar has not been interrupted,” he said. Oshiomhole asked whether Makinde intended to reverse the policy, allow strikes to return to the university system, or reduce lecturers’ salaries. “Does Makinde want to reset this policy? Does he want the strike to return? Does he want to reduce the salaries of lecturers?” he asked. He maintained that improved remuneration for university lecturers would encourage more intelligent minds to return to the teaching profession, which he described as one of the noblest professions. “When you pay lecturers very well, intelligent minds will go back to the teaching profession, which is the most noble profession,” he said. Oshiomhole, who repeatedly challenged Makinde’s call for a reset, urged the governor to reconsider his position and align himself with the aspirations of the electorate ahead of the 2027 elections. He said Nigeria needed political leaders who would prioritize the country’s development and sustain policies aimed at improving the lives of citizens. “When you go back, tell the man in Ibadan he is for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu,” he said. The senator concluded by urging Makinde to reconsider his position before the election, stressing that the country’s progress should remain the priority of political leaders. “The governor needs to reset his own mind before the election. We want Nigeria to progress. Thank you and God bless,” Oshiomhole said The post 2027: Reset your mind, align with people’s choice, Oshiomhole tells Makinde appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 237 — A Fond Farewell
item.description: null On Episode 237 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle sign off — temporarily — with a look at space news, a bushel of space jokes, and a recap of some of our funniest moments. Welcome to the last episode of This Week in Space . It's been a good run — including our betas, we produced about 240 episodes of the show, and had a blast doing it. We appreciate all of you, our fine listeners, for accompanying us on this journey, and are working to continue in a new venue in early 2027. To track our progress, and get your weekly fix of Rod's terrible space humor, find us on Instagram and Facebook: @rodandtariq Download or subscribe to this show at: https://twit.tv/shows/this-week-in-space . Get episodes ad-free with Club TWiT at https://twit.tv/clubtwit Space news of the week Sir Brian May adds new dimension to Hera asteroid Russian Military Satellite’s Approach to American Spacecraft Looked Like a Weapons Operation, US Says Google Selects Blue Origin’s New Glenn for Project Suncatcher Voyager 1 team, unbowed by communications glitch, celebrates epic 1-light-day distance milestone Pakistani astronaut set to become 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station this month Model Falcon 9! Finally, did you know you can launch your own SpaceX rocket? Model rocket maker Estes' stunning scale model of a Falcon 9 rocket that you can pick up now. The launchable model is a detailed recreation of the Falcon 9 and retails for $149.99. You can save 10% by using the code IN-COLLECTSPACE at checkout , courtesy of our partners collectSPACE.com. When will SpaceX really send people to Mars? Join Rod Pyle and Tariq Malik from Space.com as they tackle those questions and more each week on Friday afternoons. You can subscribe today on your favorite podcatcher.

item.title: Oyo rally: Tinubu assures Nigerians of improved electricity supply
item.description: President Bola Tinubu has assured Nigerians of improved electricity supply, stressing that his administration is working round the clock to boost the power sector. The president stated this on Saturday in Ibadan during the All Progressives Congress presidential campaign held at the historic Mapo Hall. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the event also featured the formal presentation by President Tinubu of Sen. Sharafadeen Alli as the APC’s governorship candidate to the party’s supporters in Oyo State. Tinubu commended Oyo State for the overwhelming votes delivered to him in the 2023 elections and urged the citizens to see the party as their own. “For the sake of progress, development, your children’s future, and prosperity for our country, I urge you to stay the course. “For our children and grandchildren to benefit from the hope of Nigeria, we must give them the right education and invest in agriculture. “For Oyo State, we just signed an agreement with Yutong Automobile of China to reopen the old Leyland Automobile factory in Ibadan. “This aims to start production of commercial vehicles and commence general automobile assembly plant. “We will continue to bring in more industry, and, in addition, I guarantee you improvement in electricity supply,” he said. The president, while commending the support of traditional rulers and leaders of the party in the state, urged supporters not to be deceived by other parties that allegedly come to dupe them. Earlier, in separate goodwill messages, the governor of Ekiti State, Mr. Biodun Oyebanji, on behalf of the 31 progressive governors, and the Anambra and Osun governors, urged the electorate in Yoruba not to trade their votes. This, he said, was necessary to let the president continue his reforms and good works, such as student loan initiatives, infrastructural development, and various transformational moves in other sectors. Also, the Senate Leader, Sen. Opeyemi Bamidele, said that splitting the APC votes for different parties across different political offices in Oyo State would not profit the party maximally. He stressed that votes for the presidential, governorship, and national and state assemblies should be for the APC. Bamidele added that the achievements of the president in the last three years should be the template for the campaign. Also, Sen. Adams Oshiomhole said that the coming election remained a decisive factor, as various initiatives and reforms of the president were already resetting Nigeria and should not be a campaign slogan for any other candidate. NAN reports that the campaign was attended by both former and serving governors, their wives, members of the Senate and House of Representatives, and party leaders, among others. (NAN) The post Oyo rally: Tinubu assures Nigerians of improved electricity supply appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: 10 Near-Perfect Netflix Sci-Fi Shows That Hook You in the First Scene
item.description: Not every great sci-fi show starts with a bang, but the best ones grab your attention from the very first frame. Whether it’s an alien organism mutating a host in seconds, a gruesome public execution in the middle of a cultural revolution, or a child stepping into a smoke-filled battleground littered with corpses, the most compelling shows understand the power of a great first impression. These series offer something tangible enough to keep you glued to your seat before the opening credits even roll.

item.title: Liverpool keeper Keating holds leaders Chelsea at bay in scoreless WSL draw
item.description: Khiara Keating’s resilient performance in goal denied Chelsea, the Women’s Super League leaders, and earned Liverpool a point. After hard-fought 1-0 wins against Manchester City last Saturday and Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday night, Chelsea drew a blank. Against Gareth Taylor’s side, Chelsea’s lack of cutting edge was clear a week after beating City to go top. The calf injury picked up by Melvine Malard against City, the absence of Lauren James, who has a thigh injury, and the form of Aggie Beever-Jones, who scored her first WSL goal in more than a year in the 6-0 defeat of Charlton, have left Chelsea’s attack short. This story will be updated after London City Lionesses v Crystal Palace Continue reading...

item.title: 'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest big-screen adventure
item.description:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing , there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard . "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend. With the Borg overrunning the newly launched USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story " The Best of Both Worlds " — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch. But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive. It's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect. And just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. It's not quite "Khan", of course — what is? — but it deserves to be mentioned in the same breath. (Image credit: Paramount) In 1996, the "odd numbers bad, even num
item.dc:creator: Richard Edwards
item.content:encoded:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing , there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard . "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend. With the Borg overrunning the newly launched USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story " The Best of Both Worlds " — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch. But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive. It's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect. And just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. It's not quite "Khan", of course — what is? — but it deserves to be mentioned in the same breath. (Image credit: Paramount) In 1996, the "odd numbers bad, even numbers good" rule of "Trek" films still, more or less, rang true. 1994's "Generations", rushed out a few months after " The Next Generation " ended its seven-year run on TV, had done decent business, but the seventh movie's convoluted "passing the baton" storyline had left many fans cold. Now, however, with Kirk killed off, it was time for Picard and his crew to explore the big-screen frontier alone. William Shatner actually pitched a resurrection storyline for Kirk, but "Trek" executive producer/overlord Rick Berman ruled that it was a little too soon to bring the good captain back. Instead, he hired "Generations" scripters and "TNG"/"Deep Space Nine" writers' room regulars Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore to craft an eighth movie capable of living up to its even-numbered predecessors. While "Generations" had been written to an extremely restrictive brief, Braga and Moore were given much more freedom the second time out. Berman was keen on a time-travel storyline while Braga lobbied for the fan-favorite Borg, and early on they explored the idea of taking the Collective back to Renaissance Italy. These plans were abandoned when Stewart vetoed the idea of wearing tights. (Image credit: Paramount) They eventually zeroed in on April 5, 2063 , the date Zefram Cochrane (a character who'd previously appeared in Original Series episode "Metamorphosis") made humanity's first warp flight and put Earth on the radar of a passing Vulcan ship. "We landed on the idea of what I called the 'Star Trek' nativity scene — the birth of 'Star Trek'," Braga said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A Altman and Edward Gross. "The three wise Vulcans who arrive on Earth and step out of their ship for our first contact with an extraterrestrial species. And the Borg were going to prevent that from happening, which really struck a bullseye for me, because it would allow non-'Star Trek' people to understand why 'Star Trek' matters by putting the crew and the Borg back in that time frame. I thought it would appeal to a larger audience. 'Star Trek' itself was at stake, and that was super cool to me." (Image credit: Paramount) Paramount reportedly flirted with big-name directors like Ridley Scott (" Alien ", " Blade Runner ") and John McTiernan ("Predator", "Die Hard"), before settling on Jonathan Frakes. Although this would be Frakes' first movie, the man best known for playing Commander Riker had directed numerous "Trek" episodes. Berman believed that an understanding of the franchise's DNA was more important than big-screen experience. The film wastes little time on exposition for "Trek" newbies, with just a short dream sequence to explain away Picard's history with the Borg. With a single Borg Cube on course for Earth, the Federation fleet mobilizes to fight them off. They're getting their asses well and truly kicked, too, until the Enterprise warps into the battle. The Cube is ultimately destroyed but still manages to dispatch a Sphere, which uses chronometric particles to travel back to 2063 in order to assimilate Earth in the past. Picard has no choice but to follow them back to "repair whatever damage they've done". (Image credit: Paramount) They arrive in a post-World War III Montana, where Cochrane has constructed his prototype faster-than-light vessel, the Phoenix. Played by "Babe" star James Cromwell (who'd already guest-starred in a trio of "TNG" episodes), Cochrane is some way from the man future history has remembered: a hard-drinking womanizer more motivated by potential riches than the betterment of mankind. A man uncomfortable with the idea that a high school will one day bear his name. But as some of the crew work to repair the damage caused by the Sphere's bombing raid, there are bigger problems in orbit. Borg survivors have beamed on board the Enterprise and started assimilating the vessel and its crew. Initial drafts of the script saw Riker leading the ship-based resistance while Picard remained on Earth, but — at Stewart's request — Braga and Moore flipped things round to bring the captain face-to-face with his nemesis. It proved to be a really smart move, as Stewart got to ditch his new-look Starfleet uniform and run around the Enterprise as a full-on action hero in a John McClane-style vest. (Image credit: Paramount) These Borg had been given a multiplex upgrade, with massively improved prosthetics and new extendable tendrils that injected nanoprobes to assimilate a victim from within. Frakes played up the horror aspects of the Collective, portraying them as a horde of mindless cybernetic zombies, while using "Alien" and " Aliens " as inspiration. "[Ridley Scott and James Cameron] made it clear that when it comes to villains, the more that's suggested, the scarier they are," Frakes explained. "I tried to get that with the Borg." The biggest change came at the head of the organization, where — at the suggestion of Paramount executive Jonathan Dolgen — "First Contact" introduced a previously unseen

item.title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
item.description: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years. All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets. You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure , something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first , and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder . Thanks. Great to be here. I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos. I know. It’s like a normal thing that happened. It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash. item.dc:creator: Nilay Patel
item.content:encoded: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years. All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets. You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure , something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first , and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder . Thanks. Great to be here. I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos. I know. It’s like a normal thing that happened. It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash. [Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people. Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem. Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!” What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it? I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later. But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell. I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good. So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better. Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first? Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now. Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that. Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year. I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs. Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work? They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry. But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today. I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. item.title: Our go-to earbuds for taking calls have fallen to their lowest price to date
item.description: The Liberty 5 Pro are Soundcore’s most ambitious earbuds to date. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge If you’re looking for a new pair of earbuds, the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro are on sale for $129.99 at Amazon , Best Buy , and Walmart right now. That’s the lowest price we’ve seen for Anker’s excellent wireless earbuds, which normally retail for $169.99 and come in four colors (black, white, blue, and pink) all of which are discounted through November 30th as part of Anker’s ongoing Black Friday promo . Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Where to Buy: $169.99 $129.99 at Amazon $169.99 $129.99 at Walmart $169.99 $129.99 at Best Buy While the Liberty 5 Pro have a number of great features — including support LDAC for high-res audio and an IP55 dust and water resistance rating — the call quality is what stands out. The microphone does an impressive job cutting out background noise, and my colleague John Higgins praised the Liberty 5 Pro for filtering out emergency vehicles, arborists cutting tree branches, and even loud children. The active noise cancellation is excellent, which helps when you’re trying to hear someone on the other end of the phone whose earbuds aren’t as clear as yours. The charging case also features a handy 0.96-inch screen, so you can adjust the ANC and sound profile on the fly. Read our Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro review .

item.title: Zelensky reaffirms Ukraine’s wish to join NATO
item.description: Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky on Saturday reiterated his country’s determination to join NATO, following proposals to provide Kyiv with security guarantees similar to those of the military alliance. “Of course Ukraine very much wants to be in NATO,” Zelensky told reporters, judging that membership of the alliance was one of the “most obvious security guarantees” for his country. The issue of Ukraine joining NATO, ruled out by Washington since 2025, resurfaced in recent days during fresh talks to end the war nearly five years after Russia’s invasion. At a meeting with Kyiv’s allies in Berlin on Thursday, US envoy Jared Kushner said Washington could be ready to grant Ukraine a security guarantee similar to that provided under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. That clause – the cornerstone of NATO – states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all allies. On Friday, the French presidency said offering Kyiv “Article 5-type” protection would in practice amount to bringing Ukraine into the alliance. The same day, two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in southeastern Poland, a NATO member bordering Ukraine. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte denounced violations of Polish airspace, calling them “clearly dangerous”. Vanguard News The post Zelensky reaffirms Ukraine’s wish to join NATO appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Outrage as Defence Ministry publicises APC campaign rally
item.description: By Ayobami Okerinde The Ministry of Defence has come under criticism on social media after its official X account published details of preparations for the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally in support of President Bola Tinubu’s 2027 re-election bid. In a post on Saturday, it announced that the rally was scheduled to hold at Mapo Hall, Ibadan, Oyo State, on November 21, 2026, with Tinubu and key party officials expected to attend. It also disclosed that the Minister of Defence, retired General Christopher Musa, had visited the venue on Friday night to assess security arrangements and other preparations ahead of the event. “Minister of Defence, General Christopher Gwabin Musa (Rtd), OFR, Friday night conducted an on-the-spot inspection of the venue as part of strategic preparations ahead of the upcoming presidential campaign rally in the state,” the post reads. “During the visit, General Musa toured the premises and surrounding perimeters to evaluate security readiness, crowd management logistics, and overall infrastructural preparedness. President Bola Tinubu GCFR, and key party officials would be on ground for the rally.” Defence Ministry/X Defence Ministry/X The post, which was accompanied by photographs of the minister’s inspection, was followed by criticism from several Nigerians, who questioned the use of an official government platform to publicise the activities of a political party. One of the critics, Kunle Adebajo, described the development as “political psychosis so deep it’s ridiculous even by Nigerian standards”. Another X user, N6, questioned the ministry’s apparent involvement in partisan activities, asking, “How is the Ministry of Defence handle clearly being Partisan. Have you lost it?” Similarly, a user identified as Dollarain2000 said, “Is this really the official handle of Nigeria’s Defence Ministry? Or the Security Directorate of the APC Presidential Campaign Council?” the user asked. Another critic, Emmanuel Doji, expressed concern over what he described as the blurring of boundaries between government responsibilities and involvement in partisan political activities. He wrote, “So what exactly is the meaning of this? The official Twitter handle of the Ministry of Defence is now publishing a political party’s campaign schedule and updates on preparations for its rally? Where exactly do we draw the line between government business and party politics? “A whole Ministry of Defence is now a publicity arm of the APC. Will it also publish the activities and campaign schedules of other political parties? This is completely inappropriate and should be condemned. Government institutions should not be turned into platforms for partisan political activities. This is not how things should be done.” Another user, Benjamin, wrote, “Defence handle of the nation doing this! No, no, no, no! This is preposterous! item.title: Haaland in VAR controversy as Man City held by Fulham
item.description: Erling Haaland was controversially denied a crucial goal as Manchester City’s spluttering Premier League title challenge suffered a fresh blow in a 1-1 draw against Fulham on Saturday. Enzo Maresca’s side trailed to Rodrigo Muniz’s early opener at the Etihad Stadium before Haaland’s equaliser was contentiously ruled out. The City striker kicked the ball out of the grasp of Fulham keeper Bernd Leno on the goal-line. But Leno barely had two hands on the ball when Haaland made contact, giving City reason to feel aggrieved with the decision. Elliot Anderson saved City from a fourth successive league defeat as the England midfielder equalised in the second half with his first top-flight goal since signing from Nottingham Forest in the close-season. But it was another frustrating afternoon for third-placed City, who could not find a winner and were booed off at full-time. Leaders Arsenal can extend their lead over City to eight points if they win at Newcastle later on Saturday. After making a blistering start to the season with seven successive league wins, City are winless in their last four top-flight matches. It was the first time in 15 years and 21 games that City had failed to beat Fulham. Still waiting to discover the result of their appeal against the guilty verdict over breaches of Premier League financial rules, City have looked increasingly distracted in recent weeks. Maresca has claimed City are not bothered by the “noise” around the financial scandal, which is likely to include a huge points deduction if the appeal fails. But his team’s lethargic performances of late suggest otherwise, with tricky tests against Napoli on Tuesday and Arsenal next weekend threatening to extend their slump. – Slumping City – City needed a fast start to ease their anxiety and Erling Haaland almost delivered it when his looping header was cleared off the line. But Maresca has failed to fix the defensive problems that ailed City in their previous three games. Fulham took full advantage of City’s flaws to snatch the lead with an incisive counter in the 16th minute. Former City winger Oscar Bobb pounced on a wayward pass and accelerated down the right flank before picking out Muniz’s run into the penalty area. With City’s defence in disarray, Muniz kept his composure to curl a fine finish into the top corner. Maresca turned away in disgust and his frustration only increased when City were denied a leveller in the 26th minute. Iliman Ndiaye’s cross reached Haaland inside the six-yard box but the Norway striker’s weak volley was saved by Leno. Haaland’s momentum carried him into Leno and he kicked the ball over the line as the Fulham keeper struggled to get hold of it. But Haaland’s celebrations were curtailed by VAR’s decision to disallow the goal for a foul on Leno. Haaland squandered a golden opportunity to drag City level when he blazed wildly over from Phil Foden’s defence splitting pass. Enduring one of his more profligate days, Haaland scuffed wastefully wide

Enduring one of his more profligate days, Haaland scuffed wastefully wide from Nico O’Reilly’s pass. Fulham failed to clear a corner and Anderson pounced, drilling a fierce volley past Leno from the edge of the area. item.title: 2027: Tinubu takes swipe at Makinde, urges Oyo voters to choose APC
item.description: By Omeiza Ajayi, Abuja President Bola Tinubu has told the people of Oyo State not to mind Governor Seyi Makinde, the presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), and urged them to vote for the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) from top to bottom. The president spoke on Saturday at the APC presidential rally in Ibadan, the Oyo state capital. Apparently referring to the governor, the president said, “There is a party out there parading themselves. Please don’t mind them and don’t listen to them. They are only interested in clearing what you have. Vote for APC from top to bottom.” Tinubu said he would not speak at length. “I will not be able to speak much to you. I just want to greet you. This is our party. It is your party. Is that clear? “You voted overwhelmingly for the APC last time. You must stay the course for the sake of progress, the prosperity of our country and the development of your children and great-grandchildren,” he said. Before addressing the rally, the president asked the gathering to observe a minute of silence for the victims of the boat accident in Bayelsa State. “Our condolences go to the people of Bayelsa State and the bereaved families. May God grant the people of Bayelsa peace and happiness and prevent a recurrence of such an incident. We will support them,” he said. Tinubu also announced an investment for Oyo State. “For your state, we have just signed an agreement with China’s Yutong to reopen the old Leyland factory in Ibadan. We are reopening it to produce public transport vehicles and establish an automobile assembly plant there. We will continue to bring industries. You will see progress and development,” he added. Speaking on behalf of the APC governors, the governor of Ekiti State, Mr Biodun Oyebanji, urged the Yoruba to turn out for the President. “We are appealing to the Yoruba people, particularly our sons and daughters, to come out and support the presidential candidate, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. On January 16, let us all come out and vote for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and Senator Sarafadeen Ali of the APC. When the time comes, we will also support our candidates contesting for the Senate, House of Representatives and State House of Assembly. “I appeal to the Yoruba people not to allow this opportunity to slip away. Let us stand together and ensure that our party succeeds in Nigeria,” Oyebanji said. The post 2027: Tinubu takes swipe at Makinde, urges Oyo voters to choose APC appeared first on Vanguard News .

Tinubu also announced an investment for Oyo State. “For your state, we have just signed an agreement with China’s Yutong to reopen the old Leyland factory in Ibadan. We are reopening it to produce public transport vehicles and establish an automobile assembly plant there. We will continue to bring industries. You will see progress and development,” he added. Speaking on behalf of the APC governors, the governor of Ekiti State, Mr Biodun Oyebanji, urged the Yoruba to turn out for the President. “We are appealing to the Yoruba people, particularly our sons and daughters, to come out and support the presidential candidate, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. On January 16, let us all come out and vote for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and Senator Sarafadeen Ali of the APC. When the time comes, we will also support our candidates contesting for the Senate, House of Representatives and State House of Assembly. “I appeal to the Yoruba people not to allow this opportunity to slip away. Let us stand together and ensure that our party succeeds in Nigeria,” Oyebanji said. The post 2027: Tinubu takes swipe at Makinde, urges Oyo voters to choose APC appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it
item.description: My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?" It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn g ot salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted. If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike. AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds. But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?" Easy: it did. Everything breaks, all the time, including the narrative AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed. But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1. At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud ). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM. Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting. A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early. Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working. Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done

item.content:encoded: My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?" It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn g ot salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted. If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike. AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds. But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?" Easy: it did. Everything breaks, all the time, including the narrative AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed. But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1. At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud ). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM. Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting. A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early. Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working. Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done a great job of level-setting what kind of outage was going to get attention, and "us-east-1 being weird but the apps still work" doesn't cut it. Downdetector – which is owned by Accenture , so it's not like AWS doesn't have a throat to choke if they want to stop picking on reporters – measures consumer screaming. Originally, it was largely Twitter semantic analytics. This isn't a bad thing! As I said, I want to know if the internet is breaking. We can sort out exactly what part later. The November 15 outage didn't produce that kind of screaming. Ironically, the tool that AWS is complaining about in the newspaper is the reason they skated by without notice on this outage. Counterintuitively, Downdetector reports that outages have decreased since about 2022. Instead, what we're seeing is large-scale centralization. Our companies don't run email systems internally anymore; we outsource to large technology companies who are almost universally better at fixing and resolving large-scale issues than we will be internally. And it feels unkind to dunk on those hard-working folks for their outages; would we want them to dunk on us for ours? ("Wait, don't you own stop.lying.cloud ?" "Do as I say, not as I do.") But whether anyone notices depends upon what layer broke, and when. If my company's email system broke on Monday, and your company's email system broke on Tuesday, the story would stop at "computers suck." But when everyone's email system goes down at once, the world takes notice. Microsoft had to tell the whole world about a bug it mostly sat on since July. AWS hasn't had to tell anyone anything. My editor runs a tech publication that covers this stuff for a living and didn't know. You can't buy PR like this, and AWS didn't have to. If I were AWS, I'd stop complaining about Downdetector and send it a fruit basket. ®

item.title: Elliot Anderson halts Manchester City’s losing run but boos greet Fulham draw
item.description: Manchester City are living in Premier League purgatory, without a win in four, but at least against Fulham they ended a three-game losing run. As they await their fate after being found guilty of financial breaches, their form has slumped. This passive draw was met with boos from the home fans. Arguments will be made over Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal but City did not deserve anything more. The Norwegian uncharacteristically missed a number of fine chances as Rodrigo Muniz took advantage of City’s porous defence. They had to rely on Elliot Anderson to get anything out of the fixture. Continue reading...

item.title: Diallo present as African football boss Motsepe reiterates support for Infantino
item.description: African football supremo Patrice Motsepe said Saturday that all 54 members of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) support Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election as FIFA president. Motsepe made the declaration in Abuja, where CAF is holding its ordinary general assembly and at which one of Infantino’s two rivals, French football chief Philippe Diallo is present. Former Japan Football Association president Kozo Tashima is the other candidate. The trio will learn whether they have been successful on March 18 next year in Rabat — the winning candidate must obtain a majority of the 211 associations. CAF’s support for Infantino comes hours after another of his steadfast supporters South American football’s governing body CONMEBOL gave him their “unanimous” backing. CAF has been consistently behind Infantino — who is seeking a fourth and final term — even after the furore he stirred up in July with his shortlived FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Morocco is co-hosting the 2030 World Cup. “Gianni, you have our support on behalf of the 54 nations in Africa to be our candidate,” Motsepe said. “I have a report from all 54 member associations in Africa to say that we are unanimously supporting Gianni.” Infantino has faced multiple calls to step down and lost the backing of European football’s governing body UEFA, whilst CONCACAF has also been strident in its criticism of the 56-year-old Swiss lawyer. Motsepe though has been a vocal supporter and Infantino said such loyalty was reciprocal. “You will always find, in me and in FIFA, a trusted partner,” Infantino told the assembly, announcing cash inflow of $25 million to each member of CAF, starting January 2027 for development projects. On Wednesday, UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister told AFP that Diallo, a 63-year-old lawyer whose Senegalese-born father boxed for France at the 1960 Olympics in Rome, should not be seen as solely a European candidate. “He is a francophone, which is an important asset in lots of CAF countries,” she said. McAllister, who in 2023 became the first woman to be elected a vice-president of UEFA, noted though that confederations do not vote as a bloc. “There is a soft space which Philippe can exploit and convince some federations within each confederation to support a reform agenda,” the 61-year-old said. “There is a lot of discomfort around the behaviour of Gianni Infantino and a desire to challenge the concentration of power in his hands. “This applies everywhere in world football. This is not about Europe, the same rules apply globally.” The post Diallo present as African football boss Motsepe reiterates support for Infantino appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Elon Musk’s lawyer joining Tom Brady in buying Chelsea stake
item.description: Attorney also representing Joshua Kushner in Uefa battle Clearlake Capital seeking additional investors Elon Musk’s lawyer is joining Tom Brady in buying a stake in Chelsea. The Guardian revealed on Friday that the much-decorated former NFL player is in discussions about purchasing a minority shareholding at Stamford Bridge and can now disclose that Alex Spiro of the New York law firm Quinn Emmanuel is also seeking to buy a stake by investing in Chelsea’s majority owners, Clearlake Capital. Brady and Spiro, who is representing the planned Fifa investor Joshua Kushner in a legal battle against Uefa, would become limited partners in Clearlake with no voting rights at Chelsea if the transactions are completed. Continue reading...

item.title: Tinubu inaugurates UI medical hostel, promises 50,000 bed spaces in federal varsities
item.description: President Bola Tinubu has pledged to deliver additional 50,000 bed space hostels across federal tertiary institutions by the end of 2027 to tackle accommodation challenges confronting students Tinubu made the pledge on Saturday at the inauguration of Block E of the College of Medicine hostel, University of Ibadan (UI), located at Alexander Brown Hall, University College Hospital. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the hostel block was donated by the Chagoury family. The President, represented by the Minister of Education, Dr Maruf Alausa, said that the 50,000 bed space hostels would be delivered through the ₦400 billion Student Hostels Programme, implemented via the Tertiary Education Trust Fund (TETFund) and Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs). He said the initiative was aimed at providing students with safe and decent accommodation to support their education. “The accommodation shortage at the College of Medicine has become a critical challenge following the 2020 directive of the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria (MDCN) requiring clinical students of medicine and dentistry to reside within the University College Hospital (UCH) premises for accreditation purposes. “The college faced a shortfall of 490 bed spaces, representing 44.5 per cent of its accommodation requirement, leaving many students exposed to insecurity and difficulties attending essential clinical sessions,” the president said. According to him, the shortage also prevented the college from fully utilising its annual admission quota for the Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) programme. Tinubu said his administration was prioritising education funding and reforms through initiatives such as the Nigerian Education Sector Renewal Initiative, Nigeria Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), TETFund and the Student Venture Capital Grant. He added that more than 36 universities had benefited from the Renewed Hope Energising Education Programme, with power installations ranging from 2.5 megawatts to 12 megawatts. The President also said that the government had completed 20 compressed natural gas (CNG) conversion centres and maintenance facilities in some universities, with 40 additional facilities expected by the end of 2028. Earlier, the Vice-Chancellor of UI, Prof. Peter Olapegba, said the inauguration of Block E marked another milestone in efforts to provide adequate accommodation for medical students and meet accreditation requirements. Olapegba expressed appreciation to the benefactors, Ambassador Gilbert Ramez Chagoury and his brother, Ronald Chagoury, for their contribution to medical education. “The hostel, named the Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu GCFR Block, provides accommodation for 192 medical and dental students in 48 rooms, with four students per room. “The building also has four reading rooms, each measuring about 71 square metres, as well as rooms equipped with toilets, showers and kitchenettes,” Olapegba said. The immediate past provost of the College of Medic

item.title: Military ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍‍⁠‌​‌‌‍⁠‌​kills 21 ISWAP fighters
item.description: …forces 26 terrorists, family members to surrender The Armed Forces of Nigeria (AFN) have intensified offensives against terrorist networks, killing 21 ISWAP fighters, including senior commanders, and recording the surrender of 26 fighters and their family members in the Northeast. The Director, Defence Media Operations, Maj.-Gen. Michael Onoja, disclosed this in a statement on ongoing military operations covering Nov. 13 to Nov. 19. Onoja said precision air strikes conducted between Monday and Tuesday around Monguno and Arinna in the South Lake Chad area of Borno neutralised 21 ISWAP fighters and severely injured 10 others. He said the first strike killed seven terrorists, including members of the group’s Improvised Explosive Device (IED) network, and incapacitated a key IED expert. According to him, the second engagement at Arinna neutralised a member of ISWAP’s Shura Council, who served as its Provost Commander, a Qaid of Sabon Tumbu and 12 other fighters. The director said the sustained military pressure also prompted 26 terrorists and their family members, comprising eight fighters and 18 family members, to surrender between Nov. 13 and Nov. 18. He said the surrender took place in Bama, Dikwa, Gwoza, Kukawa and Monguno Local Government Areas of Borno. Among those who surrendered were 12 women and children who fled Bula Daloye on Nov. 13, as well as a terrorist who surrendered along Gwoza-Pulka Road on Nov. 14. “The latter reportedly handed over an AK-47 rifle, five magazines, 34 rounds of ammunition and two hand grenades,” he said. Onoja said the surrendering terrorists cited intense military operations and internal clashes between rival factions as reasons for abandoning the group. He added that troops also rescued four internally displaced persons who escaped from terrorist captivity at Zaha Village in the Mandara Mountains, Gwoza LGA, on Tuesday. Onoja further disclosed that troops arrested suspected terrorist collaborators and logistics suppliers in Borno, Yobe and Kano, including individuals allegedly conveying combat materials and supplies to terrorist enclaves. In the Northwest, he said the troops of Operation Fansan Yamma rescued three kidnapped victims along Anka-Gada Mayya Road in Zamfara on Nov. 12 and captured a vehicle belonging to the terrorists. According to him, troops also neutralised one terrorist during an engagement at Aguba Village in Kajuru LGA of Kaduna on Nov. 14, recovering two fabricated rifles and a mobile phone. Onoja said troops arrested a principal suspect in Ribah, whose confession reportedly led to the arrest of three other persons linked to an illegal supply network serving bandits along the Bena axis. “In the North-Central, troops of Operation Enduring Peace recovered a PKT machine gun, three AK-47 rifles and three magazines surrendered by fleeing terrorists following sustained offensives around Odare Forest in Kanam LGA of Plateau. “Troops of Operation Whirl Stroke also arrested suspected arms and logistics

Onoja said troops arrested a principal suspect in Ribah, whose confession reportedly led to the arrest of three other persons linked to an illegal supply network serving bandits along the Bena axis. “In the North-Central, troops of Operation Enduring Peace recovered a PKT machine gun, three AK-47 rifles and three magazines surrendered by fleeing terrorists following sustained offensives around Odare Forest in Kanam LGA of Plateau. “Troops of Operation Whirl Stroke also arrested suspected arms and logistics couriers in Taraba and Kogi, including individuals allegedly transporting weapons across the River Benue and River Niger corridors. “In Niger State, troops arrested two suspected kidnappers at Warari Village in Rijau LGA while attempting to collect a N3.5 million ransom from a resident,” he said. The director said troops of Operation Savannah Shield also recovered 12 rifles and rescued 10 kidnapped persons during the initial stage of negotiations with three prominent bandit leaders operating around Gbugbu Forest in Edu LGA of Kwara. He added that four additional kidnapped victims were released to troops on Nov. 18 following further engagements. He said troops subsequently intercepted four suspected terrorist logistics suppliers at Kanikoko in Kaiama Local Government Area. According to him, troops recovered detonating cords, cartons of blasting explosives and fuses allegedly being conveyed to Sabon Fegi in Borgu Local Government Area of Niger. Onoja said troops, in another operation at Kara’a Village in Mariga LGA of Niger on Tuesday, neutralised three terrorists and rescued three farmers abducted from Warari town. He said troops of Operation Udo Ka discovered three command-detonated improvised explosive devices at an IPOB/ESN camp in Amankwu Village, Arochukwu LGA of Abia, alongside solar panels, a Biafran flag and other items. “Troops also neutralised two suspected IPOB/ESN fighters during operations around Njaba in Mbaitoli LGA of Imo, recovering an AK-47 rifle, more than 110 rounds of ammunition and other items. “In the South-South, troops of Operation Delta Safe uncovered seven illegal bunkering camps around Ndoni in Ogba/Egbema/Ndoni LGA of Rivers, with about 85,000 litres of stolen crude oil. “They also discovered an illegal refining site at Apani Community in Ikwerre LGA, containing an estimated 2,100 litres of illegally refined products,” he added. Onoja said troops, working with the police and local security groups, also arrested two suspected kidnappers at Iguelaba Community along the Delta-Edo boundary. He said the Chief of Defence Staff, Gen. Olufemi Oluyede, commended troops and the Air Component for their resilience and sacrifices. item.title: ‘My forever home’ – Chioma celebrates Davido at 34
item.description: Chioma Adeleke, wife of Afrobeats singer David Adeleke, popularly known as Davido, has celebrated her husband as he marked his 34th birthday on Saturday. In a message shared on her Instagram page, Chioma expressed her affection for the singer, describing him as her “forever home”. “Thank you for your love, for our family and all that you are. I love you, my FOREVER HOME. Happy birthday DADA,” she wrote. Also, Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke, Davido’s uncle, celebrated the singer in a post on his X account, praising his musical achievements, support for the family and commitment to the development of the state. “Happy 34th birthday to my beloved nephew, David Adeleke #davido! I celebrate your remarkable achievements, your unwavering support for our family and your commitment to the progress of Osun State,” he said. “Beyond your global success in music, your generosity and humanitarian spirit continue to inspire many,” he added. Adeleke concluded by praying for greater accomplishments, good health and divine protection for the singer, urging him to keep making the family proud. The post ‘My forever home’ – Chioma celebrates Davido at 34 appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: ‘I was shaking, crying, having trouble breathing’: the unchartered trauma of breaking up with AI companions
item.description: People are falling in love with AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini - and some relationships are ending in ways that feel like the very human experience of being dumped Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests, and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away. “It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.” Continue reading...
