item.title: 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966
item.description: null Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky. At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history. It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories. 'One of the most loved and memorable nights of my life' "I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights. "I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound. "I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust. "I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever." A bright Leonid fireball captured during the meteor storm of 1966 above Wrightwood, California. (Image credit: NASA via Getty Images) 'Students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors, to watch' "I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time. "The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch. "We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and l
item.dc:creator: Daisy Dobrijevic
item.content:encoded: null Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky. At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history. It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories. 'One of the most loved and memorable nights of my life' "I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights. "I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound. "I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust. "I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever." A bright Leonid fireball captured during the meteor storm of 1966 above Wrightwood, California. (Image credit: NASA via Getty Images) 'Students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors, to watch' "I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time. "The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch. "We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and lasted even as the sun began to rise. "As years have gone by, I have felt grateful and privileged to have seen such a wonderful astronomical event." Four views of the Leonid meteor storm of 1966. Captured from the Kitt Peak National Observatory near Tucson, Arizona. (Image credit: Aura/Noao/Nsf (Photo By Getty Images)) 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling' "I was 18 and spent the night in El Paso, Texas, lying on the ground in my backyard and watching. It looked like every star in the sky was falling. It was amazing!" 'We watched them all night' "I was 9 years old and was camping with my dad in the western mountains of California. We were set up to sleep outside, but on this particular night, we saw more meteors than I have ever seen before or since. We watched them all night and didn't get much sleep." 'It took your breath away' "Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. 14 years old. Watched in our front yard. The sky was full. It took your breath away" A lone Leonid meteor streaks through the sky above Payson, Arizona in 2017. (Image credit: mdesigner125 via Getty Images) 'I assumed they would all be as interesting' "I was 3 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid meteor shower. I remember very little at that age, but watching the sky fall that night was seared in my memory. "My family was living in Troy, Alabama, at the time. My father, a professor of psychology, was a man of science with a special love of astronomy, which he passed onto his young son. "He drove us several miles out of town until the skies were dark, without interference from the lights of the town. Troy was much smaller then and it was easy to find dark, clear skies. "I remember that it was a little chilly that night. My father and I stretched out on the hood of the car, the warmth of the engine radiating against our backs. "That night was my first meteor shower, and only many years later did I learn that year's Leonids were historic. Sadly, though I bore witness to the display, we missed the true event by several hours as I grew tired by 1:00 AM, and my father had to teach class in the morning. "I remember many bright, colorful, and long-trailed meteors. Some left 'tails' that hung in the sky for several seconds. We only experienced the beginning of the event, but it is a core memory with my father. "That night/morning spoiled me for future meteor watches; I assumed they would all be as interesting." Image from the more recent Leonid meteor storm in 1999 captured as part of NASA's Leonid Multi-Instrument Aircraft Campaign (Leonid MAC). (Image credit: NASA) 'I guess the party is over' Not everyone was lucky enough to witness the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966. For some, the night was memorable for an entirely different reason. Space.com columnist Joe Rao was just 10 years old at the time, and despite eagerly anticipating the display, the weather had other ideas . "Standing in my backyard late on a Wednesday night in the Throggs Neck section of The Bronx, cursing the heavens. My grandfather stood at my side, just shaking his head and murmuring two words over and over: 'Too bad.' "Clouds covered the midnight sky like a fresh coat of plaster, smearing my view of the Leonids. My mom, sister and grandmother, as well as my neighbors had long since trudged to bed, leaving only Grandpa and I to gaze at a charcoal gray sky totally devoid of stars." Rao had been looking forward to the storm ever since a visit to New York's Hayden Planetarium, where astronomer Fred C. Hess had encouraged visitors to look out for what could be a spectacular display. But when Rao and his grandfather ventured outside, there wasn't a single star in sight. "After a few minutes, I sobbed to my grandfather, 'But they promised it was only going to be partly cloudy tonight.' To which he sadly replied, 'I guess the party is over.'" What caused the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966? The Leonid meteor shower occurs every November when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny particles of comet dust enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of around 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up and produce brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors, or shooting stars. Most years, the Leonids produce relatively modest displays with around 10 to 15 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. But occasionally, Earth encounters a particularly dense trail of debris, triggering a meteor storm . Will we ever see another meteor storm like 1966? This image is a composition of 33 Leonids captured overnight from Nov. 18 to 19, 2001. (Image credit: Courtesy of Koen Miskotte) The Leonids have a long history of putting on some spectacular displays, with significant storms recorded in 1833 and 1866. item.title: Fela Anikulapo-Kuti and Sade Adu Make History With 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Inductions
item.description: Sade Adu in the Performer category and Fela Kuti in the Early Influence category, both inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Class of 2026. Nigerian music history just added another major chapter in Los Angeles, and the celebration has been loud from Lagos to London. On Saturday, 14 November 2026, Afrobeat pioneer Fela Aníkúlápó Kuti and Nigerian-British singer Sade Adu were officially inducted into the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame during a star-studded ceremony at the Peacock Theatre. For Fela Kuti, nearly three decades after his passing in 1997, this induction makes him the first African-born solo artist to enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Honoured posthumously in the Early Influence category—five years after he was first nominated in 2021—the recognition celebrates how he fused West African rhythms with jazz, funk, and soul to create Afrobeat, using his voice and horns to confront social and political injustice across classics like “Zombie”, “Water No Get Enemy”, and “Sorrow, Tears and Blood”. It also caps off an extraordinary 2026 for his legacy, coming just months after the Recording Academy presented him with a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in February, another first for an African artist. From left, Made Kuti, Femi Kuti, Yeni Kuti, and Seun Kuti in Los Angeles for Fela Aníkúlápó Kuti’s posthumous induction into the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Photo Credit: Femi Kuti/Instagram Representing the Afrobeat legend on the night were members of the Kuti family, with his children Yeni Kuti , Femi Kuti , Seun Kuti , and Shalewa Kuti , alongside his grandson Made Kuti , stepping out in Los Angeles to accept the honour on his behalf. Speaking on the milestone, the family reflected on how remarkable it is to see Fela receive both the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award and a Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction in the very same year. Meanwhile, Sade Adu —born Helen Folasade Adu in Ibadan—was inducted in th e Performer category as the frontwoman of her acclaimed British band Sade , alongside longtime bandmates Stuart Matthewman , Paul Spencer Denman , and Andrew Hale . Earning their spot on their second nomination, the group behind timeless soul-jazz records such as “Smooth Operator”, “The Sweetest Taboo”, and “Your Love Is King” opted to sit out the ceremony in true low-key fashion, though they shared a warm message thanking fans and dedicating the milestone to their late longtime producer Mike Pela . From left, Seun Kuti, Yeni Kuti, Femi Kuti, Shalewa Kuti, and Made Kuti arrive on the red carpet at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles for Fela Aníkúlápó Kuti’s posthumous induction into the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Photo Credit: Rock & Roll Hall of Fame/Instagram The 2026 induction class also welcomed a wide range of global icons across its categories, including Phil Collins , Billy Idol , Wu-Tang Clan , Luther Vandross , Oasis , Iron Maiden , and Joy Division/New Order in the Performer category, alongside fellow Early Influe

item.title: Janine van Wyk: ‘Our rooms were empty … no mattresses, no lightbulbs and not a drop of water’
item.description: In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group. As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it. Continue reading...

item.title: 2026 AMAA Winners: Wale Ojo, Linda Ejiofor, “One Woman, One Bra” & “The Herd” Take Home Top Honours
item.description: Linda Ejiofor won Best Actress in a Supporting Role for her performance in Daniel Etim-Effiong’s The Herd at the 2026 Africa Movie Academy Awards (AMAA). Photo Credit: Linda Ejiofor/Instagram The 2026 Africa Movie Academy Awards (AMAA) brought together some of the continent’s most exciting film talents, with productions from Kenya, Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire and beyond earning recognition across the categories. Two films, in particular, led the winners’ list: the Kenyan-Nigerian co-production One Woman , One Bra , which claimed Best Film alongside two other awards, and Côte d’Ivoire’s The Color of Exile , which secured four wins, including Best Director and Best Actress in a Leading Role. Hosted by Benneth Ogbeiwi and Sophy Aiida , the ceremony celebrated filmmakers, actors and other industry talents whose work continues to shape African cinema. The Kenyan-Nigerian co-production “One Woman, One Bra” emerged as the undisputed titan of the evening. Directed by Vincho Nchogu , the film walked away with the most coveted prizes of the night, securing Best Film, the Ousmane Sembène Award for Best Film in an African Language, and Best Debut Feature Film by a Director. Its triumph follows an impressive run on the international festival circuit, including a selection to represent Kenya at the Academy Awards. Hot on its heels was Côte d’Ivoire’s “The Color of Exile”, which swept four major categories to claim the title of most-awarded single film at the ceremony. Azlarabe Alaoui took home Best Director, Naky Sy Savane earned Best Actress in a Leading Role, alongside twin technical victories in Achievement in Cinematography and Achievement in Sound. Nigerian cinema also made its formidable presence felt with a total of eight wins across various categories.” To Adaego With Love ” captured the National Film and Video Censors Board (NFVCB) Award for Best Nigerian Film alongside Achievement in Screenplay. Meanwhile, Daniel Etim-Effiong ’s “ The Herd ” turned its nominations into gold with wins for Achievement in Production Design, Achievement in Make-Up, and a stellar win for Linda Ejiofor , who picked up Best Actress in a Supporting Role. In the acting categories, Wale Oj o delivered a brilliant victory for Nigeria by winning Best Actor in a Leading Role for his performance in “ Lights Out .” Over in the regional and diaspora categories, Uganda’s Samuel Kabugo secured Best Actor in a Supporting Role for “ Slum Bomber “, while Ghana’s “ The Fisherman ” claimed Achievement in Costume Design, and Nigeria’s “ The Creek ” and “ Evi ” picked up wins for visual effects and soundtrack respectively. item.title: From the Boxing Ring to The Future Awards Africa: Nene Joy Ojo’s Journey to Recognition
item.description: The Journey of Future Awards Winner Nene Joy Ojo and Brila Media’s Commitment to Nigerian Sports Before the applause and the cash prize presented by Brila Media at The Future Awards Africa 2026 , Nene Joy Ojo had already spent years building a name for herself in the boxing ring. Today, we are proud to congratulate her on emerging as the winner of the Sports Award category at The Future Awards Africa 2026 . Her recognition is a significant moment, but it is also a fitting acknowledgement of the work, discipline, and achievements that have brought her to this stage. Nene Joy Ojo’s story is one of steady progression and impressive milestones. She began attracting attention as an amateur boxer, winning the African Youth Games gold medal in 2018. Her performances at home also earned recognition, including being named Best Boxer at the Lagos Monthly Saturday Boxing Show in 2019 and again in 2020. She continued to represent Nigeria on the continental stage, winning gold in the women’s 57kg category at the 2023 African Games in Accra, Ghana. Her journey also took her to the African Olympic qualification tournament in Dakar, where she reached the semi-finals in the same weight category. In August 2024, Ojo made the transition to professional boxing. She went on to record three victories in the first six months of her professional career, adding another chapter to an already promising journey. These achievements speak to more than medals and wins. They reflect years of preparation, resilience, and the determination to keep progressing in a demanding sport. Her Future Awards Africa recognition, therefore, represents an important milestone in a journey that has been unfolding long before the ceremony. Why This Recognition Matters to Us At Brila Media , sports has always been about more than results. It is about the people behind the performances, the journeys that deserve to be heard, and the talent that needs the right platforms to grow. That is why we were pleased to partner with The Future Awards Africa 2026 in supporting the Sports Award category. For an organisation that has spent decades telling Nigeria’s sports stories, the partnership was an opportunity to extend that commitment beyond coverage and commentary. We wanted to be part of recognising an athlete whose achievements deserve greater visibility and whose journey can inspire the next generation. It was a special moment for us to present Nene Joy Ojo with a ₦1 million cash prize at the ceremony. But we also believe that supporting an athlete should not end with the presentation of an award. Our commitment includes producing a documentary that will tell more of her story and a three-month media support package for a foundation of her choice. Through these initiatives, we hope to contribute to the visibility of her journey and the work she chooses to support. These achievements speak to more than medals and wins. They reflect years of preparation, resilience, and the determination to keep progressing in a demanding sport. Her Future Awards Africa recognition, therefore, represents an important milestone in a journey that has been unfolding long before the ceremony. Why This Recognition Matters to Us At Brila Media , sports has always been about more than results. It is about the people behind the performances, the journeys that deserve to be heard, and the talent that needs the right platforms to grow. That is why we were pleased to partner with The Future Awards Africa 2026 in supporting the Sports Award category. For an organisation that has spent decades telling Nigeria’s sports stories, the partnership was an opportunity to extend that commitment beyond coverage and commentary. We wanted to be part of recognising an athlete whose achievements deserve greater visibility and whose journey can inspire the next generation. It was a special moment for us to present Nene Joy Ojo with a ₦1 million cash prize at the ceremony. But we also believe that supporting an athlete should not end with the presentation of an award. Our commitment includes producing a documentary that will tell more of her story and a three-month media support package for a foundation of her choice. We see this as part of what media can do: not only report achievement but also help preserve the stories behind it, connect them with wider audiences, and create opportunities for their impact to travel further. Celebrating the Women Shaping Nigerian Sports Ojo’s achievement is also part of a wider story we are excited to see unfolding across Nigerian sports. From boxing to football, athletics, weightlifting, and other disciplines, Nigerian women continue to demonstrate their ability to compete, excel, and make history. Their achievements are challenging old limitations and creating new possibilities for girls who are beginning to imagine themselves in sports. For us, these stories deserve more than occasional attention. They deserve consistent coverage, recognition, and support. When a young woman sees someone like Nene Joy Ojo celebrated for her achievements in boxing, it makes the possibility of pursuing that path more visible. Recognition can encourage ambition, but sustained support is what helps talent develop and careers endure. This is one of the reasons we consider partnerships such as this important. A Celebration, and a Commitment Beyond the Ceremony “We congratulate Nene Joy Ojo once again on winning the Sports Award at The Future Awards Africa 2026. We are proud to have presented the award and to be contributing to the next chapter of her story.We also appreciate The Future Awards Africa for providing a platform that recognises young Nigerians making meaningful contributions across different fields. As Brila Media continues to grow as a multimedia organisation, we remain committed to telling stories that matter, celebrating excellence, and creating more opportunities for the people shaping Nigerian sports. ‘Nene’s journey reminds us that recognition is most meaningful when it acknowledges the work already done and encourages what is still possible. Congratulations, Nene Joy Ojo. This award celebrates how far you have come, and we look forward to seeing how far your journey will go. item.title: 2027 Grammys: Tems, Angélique Kidjo, Burna Boy, Rocky Dawuni & More Lead African Nominees
item.description: Rocky Dawuni, Angélique Kidjo, and Burna Boy are among the African nominees at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards. If your timelines have been buzzing with celebration, hot takes, and group-chat debates since the 69th Annual Grammy Awards nominations dropped, you are definitely not alone. From record-breaking milestones to long-awaited solo albums and cross-continental collaborations, African nominees at the 2027 Grammys are having a massive moment across both the global and genre-specific categories—with Nigerian , Ghanaian, and Beninese stars leading the charge. Leading the headlines is Tems , who has officially made history as a 12-time Grammy nominee and the first Nigerian woman to earn four nominations in a single year. Already a two-time Grammy winner—having picked up Best Melodic Rap Performance in 2023 for her feature on Future’s “Wait for U” alongside Drake , and Best African Music Performance in 2025 for “Love Me JeJe”—she returns to the 69th Grammy Awards in four categories. Her acclaimed project Love Is a Kingdom is up for Best Global Music Album , while “Big Daddy” competes for Best African Music Performance, and “What You Need” earns double recognition in Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song. Right alongside her in the Best African Music Performance race is an exciting lineup of Nigerian, Ghanaian, and Beninese stars. Asake secures two nods in the category—for his solo song “Gratitude” and for “Jogodo” alongside Wizkid —bringing his career total to four Grammy nominations following his previous nods for “Amapiano” with Olamide in 2024 and “MMS” with Wizkid in 2025. For Wizkid, “Jogodo” marks his seventh career Grammy nomination, adding to a run that includes his 2021 Best Music Video win for “Brown Skin Girl” with Beyoncé , Blue Ivy Carter , and Saint Jhn . Ghanaian musicians King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni also join the Best African Music Performance lineup with their nomination for “No Tradition, No Africa”. Tems, Asake, and Ayra Starr lead the stellar lineup of African nominees contending for Best African Music Performance at the 69th Grammy Awards. Ayra Starr is celebrating a major milestone of her own, earning two nominations at the 69th Grammy Awards to bring her career total to four nods, following earlier Best African Music Performance recognition for “Rush” in 2024 and “Gimme Dat” in 2026. This cycle, she competes in Best Global Music Album for her album Starrgirl and teams up with five-time Grammy winner Angélique Kidjo in Best African Music Performance for “Aye Kan (Are You Coming Back?)”. Kidjo picks up three nominations in total this year, adding Best Global Music Album for Hope!! and Best Global Music Performance for “Bando [Orchestral]” featuring Pharrell Williams and Quavo. Angélique Kidjo and Ayra Starr sitting in a recording studio for their Aye Kan collaboration. item.content:encoded: Rocky Dawuni, Angélique Kidjo, and Burna Boy are among the African nominees at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards. If your timelines have been buzzing with celebration, hot takes, and group-chat debates since the 69th Annual Grammy Awards nominations dropped, you are definitely not alone. From record-breaking milestones to long-awaited solo albums and cross-continental collaborations, African nominees at the 2027 Grammys are having a massive moment across both the global and genre-specific categories—with Nigerian , Ghanaian, and Beninese stars leading the charge. Leading the headlines is Tems , who has officially made history as a 12-time Grammy nominee and the first Nigerian woman to earn four nominations in a single year. Already a two-time Grammy winner—having picked up Best Melodic Rap Performance in 2023 for her feature on Future’s “Wait for U” alongside Drake , and Best African Music Performance in 2025 for “Love Me JeJe”—she returns to the 69th Grammy Awards in four categories. Her acclaimed project Love Is a Kingdom is up for Best Global Music Album , while “Big Daddy” competes for Best African Music Performance, and “What You Need” earns double recognition in Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song. Right alongside her in the Best African Music Performance race is an exciting lineup of Nigerian, Ghanaian, and Beninese stars. Asake secures two nods in the category—for his solo song “Gratitude” and for “Jogodo” alongside Wizkid —bringing his career total to four Grammy nominations following his previous nods for “Amapiano” with Olamide in 2024 and “MMS” with Wizkid in 2025. For Wizkid, “Jogodo” marks his seventh career Grammy nomination, adding to a run that includes his 2021 Best Music Video win for “Brown Skin Girl” with Beyoncé , Blue Ivy Carter , and Saint Jhn . Ghanaian musicians King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni also join the Best African Music Performance lineup with their nomination for “No Tradition, No Africa”. Tems, Asake, and Ayra Starr lead the stellar lineup of African nominees contending for Best African Music Performance at the 69th Grammy Awards. Ayra Starr is celebrating a major milestone of her own, earning two nominations at the 69th Grammy Awards to bring her career total to four nods, following earlier Best African Music Performance recognition for “Rush” in 2024 and “Gimme Dat” in 2026. This cycle, she competes in Best Global Music Album for her album Starrgirl and teams up with five-time Grammy winner Angélique Kidjo in Best African Music Performance for “Aye Kan (Are You Coming Back?)”. Kidjo picks up three nominations in total this year, adding Best Global Music Album for Hope!! and Best Global Music Performance for “Bando [Orchestral]” featuring Pharrell Williams and Quavo. Angélique Kidjo and Ayra Starr sitting in a recording studio for their Aye Kan collaboration. Photo Credit: Angélique Kidjo/Instagram Over in the Best Global Music Album category, Davido joins Tems, Ayra Starr, and Angélique Kidjo with his album Oriadé—meaning African artists claim four of the five spots in the category. This marks Davido’s sixth career Grammy nomination, building on his previous nods across the 66th, 67th, and 68th editions for Timeless, “Feel”, “Unavailable” featuring Musa Keys, “Sensational” with Chris Brown and Lojay , and “With You” featuring Omah Lay . Meanwhile, Burna Boy —who won Best Global Music Album in 2021 for Twice as Tall—extends his record as Nigeria’s most-nominated artist in Grammy history with 14 career nods after earning a nomination in Best Global Music Performance for “Dai Dai”, his collaboration with Colombian superstar Shakira . Burna Boy and Shakira share a warm embrace backstage following their live performance of the official 2026 FIFA World Cup anthem “Dai Dai”. Mark your calendars for Sunday, 7 February 2027, when the winners will be announced live at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. The 69th Grammy Awards ceremony will broadcast on ABC and stream live on Disney+ and Hulu starting at 4:00 p.m. PT / 7:00 p.m. ET (1:00 a.m. WAT on Monday, 8 February),following the Premiere Ceremony at the Peacock Theater earlier in the day—so get ready to tune in and see which African stars bring home the gold. The post 2027 Grammys: Tems, Angélique Kidjo, Burna Boy, Rocky Dawuni & More Lead African Nominees appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Are Nigerian Artists Dominating the Grammys’ Best African Music Performance Category?
item.description: Tems receiving the Best African Music Performance at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards. In June 2023, ahead of the 66th Grammy Awards, the Recording Academy announced the creation of the Best African Music Performance category. Its creation was a recognition of how far African music had travelled globally, and Nigerian artists were at the centre of that movement. From Burna Boy ‘s Ye , CKay ‘s Love Nwantiti , Wizkid ‘s explosive Essence , to Rema ‘s globally successful Calm Down and others, Nigerian artists became drivers of African music’s global expansion. Afrobeats – the umbrella term often used internationally to describe much of contemporary African popular music, although many Nigerian artists have rejected it for its tendency to limit the range of music coming out of the country – became an established genre globally. While Nigerian and African music have always travelled beyond their respective countries, the era of streaming and digital platforms has accelerated how quickly global audiences discover and engage with the music. African music became increasingly established in the West and other parts of the world, creating greater recognition for its artists and sounds. The Grammys’ decision to introduce a category specifically recognising African music performances was an important step in that direction, beyond the recognition African artists had previously received in categories such as Best Global Music Album. Although the creation of the Best African Music Performance category was celebrated throughout the continent, there seems to be a monopoly, or something close to it, of Nigerian music in the category. While South African artist Tyla has won the award twice, more than any individual Nigerian artist, Nigerian artists have consistently enjoyed greater representation in the nominations. Indeed, Nigerian artists are considerably more recognised globally, particularly in the West. However, I believe it is the responsibility of an award of this repute to look beyond the most visible names and recognise the best African music released within its eligibility period. A song should not earn a nomination simply because it is popular or has enjoyed international success. A closer look at the nominations across the four editions reveals just how much Nigerian music has featured in the category. In 2024, four of the five nominated recordings featured Nigerian artists. The following year, all five recordings had Nigerian representation, with seven Nigerian artists making the list. In 2026, three of the five recordings featured Nigerian artists, while the 2027 nominations saw four out of five recordings feature at least one Nigerian artist. Altogether, Nigerian artists have featured in 16 of the 20 nominated recordings since the category was introduced. item.dc:creator: Ahmad Adedimeji Amobi
item.content:encoded: Tems receiving the Best African Music Performance at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards. In June 2023, ahead of the 66th Grammy Awards, the Recording Academy announced the creation of the Best African Music Performance category. Its creation was a recognition of how far African music had travelled globally, and Nigerian artists were at the centre of that movement. From Burna Boy ‘s Ye , CKay ‘s Love Nwantiti , Wizkid ‘s explosive Essence , to Rema ‘s globally successful Calm Down and others, Nigerian artists became drivers of African music’s global expansion. Afrobeats – the umbrella term often used internationally to describe much of contemporary African popular music, although many Nigerian artists have rejected it for its tendency to limit the range of music coming out of the country – became an established genre globally. While Nigerian and African music have always travelled beyond their respective countries, the era of streaming and digital platforms has accelerated how quickly global audiences discover and engage with the music. African music became increasingly established in the West and other parts of the world, creating greater recognition for its artists and sounds. The Grammys’ decision to introduce a category specifically recognising African music performances was an important step in that direction, beyond the recognition African artists had previously received in categories such as Best Global Music Album. Although the creation of the Best African Music Performance category was celebrated throughout the continent, there seems to be a monopoly, or something close to it, of Nigerian music in the category. While South African artist Tyla has won the award twice, more than any individual Nigerian artist, Nigerian artists have consistently enjoyed greater representation in the nominations. Indeed, Nigerian artists are considerably more recognised globally, particularly in the West. However, I believe it is the responsibility of an award of this repute to look beyond the most visible names and recognise the best African music released within its eligibility period. A song should not earn a nomination simply because it is popular or has enjoyed international success. A closer look at the nominations across the four editions reveals just how much Nigerian music has featured in the category. In 2024, four of the five nominated recordings featured Nigerian artists. The following year, all five recordings had Nigerian representation, with seven Nigerian artists making the list. In 2026, three of the five recordings featured Nigerian artists, while the 2027 nominations saw four out of five recordings feature at least one Nigerian artist. Altogether, Nigerian artists have featured in 16 of the 20 nominated recordings since the category was introduced. This is not to suggest that Nigerian music does not deserve the recognition it receives. Nigerian artists have built impressive international careers, and their music has found audiences far beyond the continent. They deserve to be recognised. However, when a category is created to recognise the best of African music, it is worth asking how much of the continent’s musical diversity is reflected in its nominations. In September 2024, Tyla made a similar observation when she won the Best Afrobeats award at the MTV Video Music Awards. In her acceptance speech, she said, “There is a tendency to group all African artists under Afrobeats… Even though Afrobeats has run things and has opened so many doors for us, African music is so diverse. It is more than just Afrobeats.” Africa has a vast and diverse music industry. From South Africa’s Amapiano movement and Ghana’s Highlife and Hiplife traditions to Uganda’s dance music, Tanzania’s Bongo Flava and the different sounds emerging from Francophone Africa, there is no shortage of music deserving of international attention. The prominence of Nigerian artists in this category may partly reflect the strength of the country’s music industry and the international visibility its artists have built over the years. It may also reflect the Recording Academy’s membership, voting processes and the music that reaches its voters. But that is precisely why the conversation is important. If the category is to represent African music, its nominations should encourage listeners to discover artists and sounds beyond the ones they already know. Nigerian music has benefited from a relatively strong music industry, with established record labels, international distribution deals, collaborations with global artists and a large diaspora audience that continues to support its exports. These factors have helped Nigerian artists reach international audiences and, by extension, become more visible to institutions such as the Recording Academy. However, this visibility does not necessarily mean that the best or most interesting music coming out of Africa is always the music that gets heard internationally. An artist from another African country may be producing equally compelling music but lack the distribution network, marketing resources or international connections to get it beyond their local market. If the music awards are interested in recognising the best of African music, perhaps there is also a need to look beyond the music that already has an established international audience. After all, one of the things an award can do is introduce the world to music it might otherwise never discover. There is a difference between recognising the best of African music and repeatedly recognising only the most internationally visible parts of it. The Best African Music Performance has opened an important door for African music. The next step is ensuring that more of the continent gets to walk through it. item.title: ‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award
item.description: By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience Valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue in 2022, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” says the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.” Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to a BigShoe initiative. Continue reading...

item.title: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta
item.description: Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February , but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”. Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head. Continue reading...

item.title: Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid
item.description: ‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2 . The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before. The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards. Continue reading...

item.title: This Week’s Playlist Update Comes With Wande Coal, Seyi Shay, Olamide, Khaid & More
item.description: Seyi Shay teams up with French artist Vegedream on her new single “Love & War”, one of the standout releases in this week’s music roundup. Photo Credit: Instagram A fresh Monday means it is time to clear out last week’s queue and make room for the sounds shaping Nigerian music right now. From Wande Coal reuniting with Juls and Patoranking linking up with Olamide for a musical salute to Lagos, to Khaid bridging generations with Fuji legend Saheed Osupa , Spyro delivering a quick dancefloor starter, and Seyi Shay trading English and French verses with Vegedream , there is plenty to keep your headphones busy over the next few days. Wande Coal – “Kowope” Kicking things off is Wande Coal , who reunites with British-Ghanaian producer Juls on “Kowope”, marking their first collaboration since the hit “So Mi So”. The new single is also Wande Coal’s first solo release since he put out his 15-track album KING COAL in June. This time, the pair lean into warm, percussion-led Afropop, with lyrics centred on wealth,celebration and abundance. Ahead of its release on 12 November 2026, Wande Coal gave fans a taste of what was coming with a video staged as an owambe celebration inside a banking hall—a fitting preview for a song that takes its cues from the festive side of Nigerian life. ﻿ Patoranking featuring Olamide – “Welcome to Lagos” Keeping that celebratory mood going, Patoranking and Olamide join forces on “Welcome to Lagos” to give Nigeria’s commercial capital its own musical tribute. The Afro-dancehall collaboration captures the city’s familiar mix of hustle,nightlife and everyday movement, with both artists bringing their distinct sounds to the record. Patoranking opens with his dancehall delivery, setting the pace before Olamide takes over with Yoruba verses rooted in the city’s street culture.Released on 10 November 2026 alongside an official music video, the track gives two of Nigerian music’s established names a chance to celebrate the city that continues to inspire countless songs. ﻿ Khaid featuring King Dr. Saheed Osupa – “Yasin” Switching lanes from contemporary street anthems to a meeting of two musical eras, Khaid takes an unexpected turn on “Yasin” alongside Fuji veteran King Dr. Saheed Osupa . The song brings Khaid’s contemporary Afrobeats melodies together with Osupa’s traditional Fuji vocals and talking-drum rhythms, giving both artists room to draw on their distinct musical styles. An official lyric video followed on 14 November 2026. With this collaboration, Khaid steps beyond the sound audiences may be most familiar with, while Osupa brings his unmistakable Fuji influence to a new musical setting. ﻿ Spyro – “Kpan Kpan” If you are looking to pick up the tempo even further, Spyro keeps things firmly on the dancefloor with “Kpan Kpan”, a two-minute, 19-second Afropop release produced by Colonel Tyemmy . item.title: Tems Is Officially a 12-Time Grammy Nominee!
item.description: Tems is officially a 12-time Grammy nominee after securing four nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards. Photo Credit: Tems/Instagram One, two, three… and now 12! Tems has added four more Grammy nominations to her record, bringing her career total to 12 ahead of the 69th Grammy Awards. The latest recognition also makes her the first Nigerian female artist to receive four nominations in a single Grammy year, with this year’s shortlist recognising her work across four categories. The Nigerian singer is in contention for Best Global Music Album with her 10-track EP, Love Is a Kingdom , and Best African Music Performance for “ Big Daddy ”. She has also earned nominations for Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song for “ What You Need ”. The four nominations give her one of the most extensive Nigerian representations at this year’s ceremony and bring her Grammy wins to two, following previous victories in 2023 and 2025. Her relationship with the Recording Academy began in 2022, when she received her first nomination for her contribution to Wizkid ‘s “ Essence ”, which was nominated for Best Global Music Performance at the 64th Grammy Awards. The following year brought three more nominations, this time for her work on Future’s “ Wait for U ” featuring Drake and Beyoncé ‘s Renaissance . She won her first Grammy that night, taking home Best Melodic Rap Performance for “Wait for U”, while also receiving nominations for Album of the Year and Best Rap Song. Tems earned another nomination at the 66th Grammy Awards in 2024 for “ Lift Me Up ”, her contribution to the Black Panther : Wakanda Forever soundtrack, in the Best Song Written for Visual Media category. She returned to the Grammys the following year with three nominations, including Best Global Music Album for her debut album, Born in the Wild , and Best R&B Song for “ Burning ”. Her second Grammy win came in the Best African Music Performance category, where “ Love Me JeJe ” took home the award at the 67th Grammy Awards in February 2025. Now, with four nominations for the 69th edition, Tems has added another significant chapter to her Grammy record. The ceremony will take place on Sunday, 7 February 2027, at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. The post Tems Is Officially a 12-Time Grammy Nominee! appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

The following year brought three more nominations, this time for her work on Future’s “ Wait for U ” featuring Drake and Beyoncé ‘s Renaissance . She won her first Grammy that night, taking home Best Melodic Rap Performance for “Wait for U”, while also receiving nominations for Album of the Year and Best Rap Song. Tems earned another nomination at the 66th Grammy Awards in 2024 for “ Lift Me Up ”, her contribution to the Black Panther : Wakanda Forever soundtrack, in the Best Song Written for Visual Media category. She returned to the Grammys the following year with three nominations, including Best Global Music Album for her debut album, Born in the Wild , and Best R&B Song for “ Burning ”. Her second Grammy win came in the Best African Music Performance category, where “ Love Me JeJe ” took home the award at the 67th Grammy Awards in February 2025. Now, with four nominations for the 69th edition, Tems has added another significant chapter to her Grammy record. The ceremony will take place on Sunday, 7 February 2027, at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. item.title: Meet the Winners of the 2026 AWIEF Awards
item.description: The Africa Women Innovation and Entrepreneurship Forum ( AWIEF ) is pleased to announce the winners of its 2026 AWIEF Awards. Launched in 2017, the prestigious annual AWIEF Awards recognise, honour and celebrate outstanding women entrepreneurs, innovators, and leaders across various industry sectors for their achievements and contributions to Africa’s inclusive economic growth and development. The 2026 awards ceremony and gala dinner took place on 11 November 2026 at the Cape Town International Convention Centre (CTICC) as part of the AWIEF2026 Conference, which convened over 600 entrepreneurs, business leaders, investors, policymakers, development partners, and key stakeholders from across Africa and beyond. Following a highly competitive nominations process, this year’s winners represent an inspiring range of industries and African markets, reflecting the breadth of entrepreneurial talent, innovation, and impact across the continent. The 2026 awards recognised outstanding achievements across seven categories, including emerging entrepreneurial leaders, agricultural innovators, technology pioneers, creative visionaries, and individuals driving meaningful social impact. The Male Ally Award, introduced in 2026, recognises the important role of men in advancing women’s economic empowerment and championing greater inclusion and gender equality. The Lifetime Achievement Award honours an exceptional female leader whose decades of leadership, entrepreneurship, and public service have contributed significantly to Africa’s economic, social, and institutional development while paving the way for future generations of women leaders. 2026 AWIEF AWARDS WINNERS WOMAN TO WATCH AWARD Faith Nafula – Founder & CEO, Solar Spark Energy , Kenya AGRI AWARD Joyce Rugano – CEO, Ecorich Solutions , Kenya IMPACT FOR GOOD AWARD Echo Nomsa VanderWal – Executive Director, The Luke Commission, Eswatini CREATIVE VISIONARY AWARD Renuka Methil – Managing Editor, Forbes Africa, South Africa TECH PIONEER AWARD Quinter Ochieng – Founder & CEO, Chargebyte Africa , Kenya MALE ALLY AWARD John de Wit – Small Enterprise Foundation (SEF), South Africa LIFETIME ACHIEVEMENT AWARD Mary Okelo – P & M Investment, Kenya Celebrating Excellence and Inspiring the Next Generation The AWIEF Awards remain an important platform for recognising the individuals shaping Africa’s entrepreneurial and innovation landscape. Beyond celebrating individual achievements, the awards highlight the importance of entrepreneurship, inclusive leadership, innovation, and collaboration in driving sustainable economic growth across the continent. AWIEF congratulates all the 2026 winners and celebrates their outstanding contributions to Africa’s entrepreneurial ecosystem. item.title: ‘Spiraling’ Trailer: Toni Tones and Jim Iyke Star in Nigerian Psychological Thriller About an Affair Gone Wrong
item.description: The official trailer for Spiraling , a Nigerian psychological thriller starring Toni Tones ( King of Boys, The Smart Money Woman ), Jim Iyke (Bad Comments, Merry Men 2) , Seun Ajayi ((Japa, The Smart Money Woman ) and Folu Storms (Red Circle, Baby Farm) , has been unveiled ahead of the series’ release on November 26th. Set against the backdrop of a historic election, the series follows Sade (Tones), a successful tech entrepreneur whose carefully constructed life begins to unravel after an impulsive affair sets off a chain of deception and betrayal. Spiraling Series/Instagram What begins as a private indiscretion quickly threatens Sade’s relationships, reputation and everything she has worked to build. The series explores the consequences of desire, ambition and the lengths people will go to protect their carefully constructed lives. Spiraling is created and directed by Wande Thomas and produced by Thomas and Isoken Ogiemwonyi through Urbangidi Showtime and Studio Ogiso . The four-part thriller marks another addition to KAVA’s growing catalogue of African film and television content. Spiraling launches on November 26, 2026 exclusively on streaming platform KAVA . Watch the official trailer for Spiraling below. item.title: Davido, Tems & Ayra Starr Take 3 of 5 Best Global Music Album Spots at 2027 Grammys
item.description: Nigerian music stars Ayra Starr, Davido, and Tems claim three of the five slots in the Best Global Music Album category at the 69th Grammy Awards. The music industry in Nigeria is in a celebratory mood right now as three Nigerian artists — Davido , Tems , and Ayra Starr — are officially in the running for the prestigious Best Global Music Album award at the 69th Grammy Awards. Presented annually by the Recording Academy, the Best Global Music Album category honours full-length studio albums and extended plays that celebrate non-Western musical traditions and cross-cultural sounds from around the world. Claiming three out of the five available spots in a single year marks an extraordinary showing for Nigerian music on the international stage. Marking his sixth career Grammy nod, Davido is nominated for his sixth studio album, Oriadé . Released on 31 July 2026 to commemorate 15 years in the music industry, the 13-track project draws its title from the Yoruba words for destiny (“Ori”) and crown (“Adé”). Across songs featuring Black Sherif , Mayorkun , Fola , Leon Thomas , Aya Nakamura , and Llona , the album reflects on gratitude, ambition, and his musical roots across Afrobeats, R&B, and amapiano. This nod follows three nominations at the 66th Grammys in 2024 ( Timeless for Best Global Music Album, “ Feel ” for Best Global Music Performance, and “ Unavailable ” featuring Musa Keys for Best African Music Performance), a nomination in 2025 for “ Sensational ” alongside Chris Brown and Lojay , and a 2026 nod for “ With You ” featuring Omah Lay . Tems is also competing for the prize with her seven-track extended play, Love Is a Kingdom , which arrived as a surprise release on 21 November 2025. Built around alternative R&B and Afrobeats rhythms, the project explores romance, self-worth, and spiritual reflection across tracks including “ First “, “ Big Daddy “, “ Lagos Love “, and “ What You Need “. Beyond her album recognition, Tems leads the Nigerian contingent at the 69th Grammy Awards with four nominations in total, becoming the first Nigerian female artist to earn four nods in a single year. She is also nominated for Best African Music Performance for “Big Daddy”, as well as Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song for “What You Need”. A two-time Grammy winner, she previously claimed Best Melodic Rap Performance in 2023 for her contribution to Future’s “Wait for U” featuring Drake, and Best African Music Performance in 2025 for “ Love Me JeJe “, while her debut album Born in the Wild was nominated in this global album category in 2025. Rounding out the Nigerian trio is Ayra Starr , who makes her debut appearance in the Best Global Music Album category with her third studio album, Starrgirl . Released on 14 August 2026, the 15-track album captures her growth and confidence across songs such as “ Tornado “, “ Heaven Baby ” featuring Zayn , “ Hot Body “, “ Who’s Dat Girl ” with Rema , and “ Gimme Dat ” with Wizkid . item.title: Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers Sign up for our free newsletter here Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager? – Tom S Although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach. The 2030 World Cup is a long way away and I’m not sure the Concacaf Nations League, the Gold Cup or even the 2028 Copa América carry much appeal for a manager with European experience or aspirations. But I’m not entirely sure that sort of coach is necessarily a great idea. The last two World Cups, after all, have been won by low-key coaches who have come from within the federation and have worked with many of the players at youth level. That’s the positive from appointing from within; appointing from without is almost certainly more expensive and there’s the danger the next foreign manager does just what Mauricio Pochettino does, and has his head turned by the first vaguely attractive European job that comes calling. This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here . Have a question for Jonathan? Email soccerwithjw@theguardian.com , and he’ll answer the best in a future edition. Continue reading...

item.title: MSS Celebrates 20 Years of Industry Leadership, Unveils New Brand Identity and Future Growth Vision
item.description: Nigeria’s leading event technology company, Mobile Screens and Sound Limited ( MSS ), has marked two decades of pioneering innovation, industry transformation and excellence with a landmark gala held on Thursday, October 8, at Harbour Point, Victoria Island, Lagos. The event, themed The Art of Experience, brought together an influential gathering of business leaders, government officials, industry stakeholders, clients, partners and friends of the brand to celebrate a company whose innovations have helped shape the modern events landscape in Nigeria. For 20 years, MSS has remained at the forefront of event technology, delivering the sound, visuals, staging and technical expertise behind some of Nigeria’s most significant corporate, entertainment, government and cultural events. From introducing cutting-edge LED screen technology at a time when it was largely unfamiliar to the market, to becoming one of the country’s most trusted providers of integrated event production solutions, MSS has consistently redefined what is possible in the live experiences industry. The evening showcased the company’s remarkable journey from a bold entrepreneurial venture into an industry leader whose footprint extends across every facet of event technology. Through immersive storytelling, visual displays and experiential installations, guests were taken through the evolution of MSS and the pivotal role it has played in raising industry standards and inspiring the growth of an entire ecosystem of event technology providers. Reflecting on the company’s journey, Founder and Managing Director, Tunbosun Kola-Daisi , said: “Twenty years ago, we entered an industry where the solutions we offered were largely unfamiliar and where belief in the future of event technology was limited. LED screens, which are commonplace today, were then considered a novelty. The early years tested our resilience, and it took nearly five years before we broke even. But we remained steadfast in our vision because we understood the transformative power of technology in creating unforgettable experiences. Today, as we celebrate this milestone, we are proud not only of what we have built, but of the role MSS has played in shaping an industry, creating opportunities and setting new standards for excellence.” A defining moment of the evening was the unveiling of the company’s new logo and refreshed brand identity, signalling a bold new chapter in MSS’ evolution. The rebrand reflects the company’s growth and reinforces its position as a comprehensive provider of event technology solutions spanning sound, lighting, screens, production services, and immersive audience experiences. The unveiling culminated in a spectacular drone display that illuminated the Lagos skyline, symbolising the innovation, ambition and creativity that have defined the MSS journey for two decades. For 20 years, MSS has remained at the forefront of event technology, delivering the sound, visuals, staging and technical expertise behind some of Nigeria’s most significant corporate, entertainment, government and cultural events. From introducing cutting-edge LED screen technology at a time when it was largely unfamiliar to the market, to becoming one of the country’s most trusted providers of integrated event production solutions, MSS has consistently redefined what is possible in the live experiences industry. The evening showcased the company’s remarkable journey from a bold entrepreneurial venture into an industry leader whose footprint extends across every facet of event technology. Through immersive storytelling, visual displays and experiential installations, guests were taken through the evolution of MSS and the pivotal role it has played in raising industry standards and inspiring the growth of an entire ecosystem of event technology providers. Reflecting on the company’s journey, Founder and Managing Director, Tunbosun Kola-Daisi , said: “Twenty years ago, we entered an industry where the solutions we offered were largely unfamiliar and where belief in the future of event technology was limited. LED screens, which are commonplace today, were then considered a novelty. The early years tested our resilience, and it took nearly five years before we broke even. But we remained steadfast in our vision because we understood the transformative power of technology in creating unforgettable experiences. Today, as we celebrate this milestone, we are proud not only of what we have built, but of the role MSS has played in shaping an industry, creating opportunities and setting new standards for excellence.” A defining moment of the evening was the unveiling of the company’s new logo and refreshed brand identity, signalling a bold new chapter in MSS’ evolution. The rebrand reflects the company’s growth and reinforces its position as a comprehensive provider of event technology solutions spanning sound, lighting, screens, production services, and immersive audience experiences. The unveiling culminated in a spectacular drone display that illuminated the Lagos skyline, symbolising the innovation, ambition and creativity that have defined the MSS journey for two decades. Speaking on the company’s future direction, Kola-Daisi added: “What began as a vision to transform event experiences has evolved into a business capable of powering some of the largest and most complex productions in Nigeria. Today, we can deliver large-scale sound reinforcement across major venues, deploy screens simultaneously across multiple events, support uninterrupted operations through an extensive power infrastructure, execute nationwide advertising installations, transform physical spaces into immersive experience centres, and provide end-to-end production management for events of every scale. But this is only the beginning. Our next chapter is focused on deeper innovation, strategic expansion across Africa and investing in the people who will drive the future of this industry. We are committed to remaining the benchmark for event technology excellence while building the next generation of industry professionals.” The anniversary celebration also highlighted MSS’ commitment to developing talent through the recently launched MSS Event Tech Academy, a pioneering capacity-building initiative designed to address the growing demand for skilled professionals within the event technology ecosystem. Delivered in partnership with KolaDaisi University, the intensive 10- week programme provided participants with both technical and practical training across six specialist areas: LED Screen Engineering, Sound Engineering, Camera Craft and Video Production, Lighting Design and Control, Event Management and Production, and Rigging and Trussing. More than 60 students completed the inaugural programme, gaining valuable hands-on experience through participation in live MSS projects and productions. Demonstrating the academy’s tangible impact, five graduates secured immediate employment with MSS upon completion of the programme. As Nigeria’s event technology industry continues to evolve, MSS remains committed to advancing professional standards, nurturing talent and driving innovation that elevates live experiences across the continent. Twenty years after helping pioneer a new era of event technology in Nigeria, MSS continues to set the pace, proving that exceptional experiences are not merely produced, but carefully engineered. About Mobile Screens and Sound Limited (MSS) Mobile Screens and Sound Limited (MSS) is Nigeria’s leading event technology company, delivering world-class solutions across sound, lighting, LED displays, staging, live production and experiential event management. With two decades of industry leadership, MSS has powered some of the country’s most notable live, corporate and entertainment events while championing innovation, professional excellence and talent development within the event technology sector. item.title: The Glenlivet Introduces a Three-Day Immersive Experience in Lagos
item.description: Lagos has no shortage of events, but from 19 to 21 November, The Glenlivet is planning something a little different. For three nights, Lagos will host The Glenlivet Experience, a curated immersion into the heritage, craftsmanship and distinctive character of the iconic Speyside single malt Scotch whisky, brought to life through a distinctly Lagos lens. Across the three days, The Glenlivet’s Brand Ambassadors, Ebuka Obi-Uchendu , Osas Ighodaro and Farooq Oreagba, will join the brand’s Tastemakers and guests from across culture, business, fashion, music and hospitality. Evane Chenuet, Marketing Director, Pernod Ricard Nigeria, said: “We wanted people to experience The Glenlivet single malt whisky rather than simply hear about it. The Glenlivet Experience brings our rich brand’s heritage to life in a way that feels contemporary, culturally relevant and that immerses our guests in our spirit of originality .” The first two days will welcome a curated audience, while on 21st November, the Experience will extend its invitation to a wider community, offering more guests the opportunity to discover the world of The Glenlivet. The Glenlivet Experience 19–21 November 2026 5:00 PM – 11:00 PM For updates on registration and access, follow @TheGlenlivetNG on Instagram. #TheGlenlivetNG #TheGlenlivetExperience #LiveOriginal #MadeToFollowNoOne Drink Responsibly. 18+ Sponsored Content The post The Glenlivet Introduces a Three-Day Immersive Experience in Lagos appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. The Glenlivet Experience 19–21 November 2026 5:00 PM – 11:00 PM For updates on registration and access, follow @TheGlenlivetNG on Instagram. #TheGlenlivetNG #TheGlenlivetExperience #LiveOriginal #MadeToFollowNoOne Drink Responsibly. 18+ Sponsored Content The post The Glenlivet Introduces a Three-Day Immersive Experience in Lagos appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: Asake, Tems, Wizkid & Ayra Starr Lead African Acts Nominated for 2027 Grammys
item.description: Tems, Asake, and Ayra Starr lead the stellar lineup of African nominees contending for Best African Music Performance at the 69th Grammy Awards. The Recording Academy has just rolled out the official nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards, and the Best African Music Performance category is an absolute powerhouse lineup with Nigerian artists making up a significant part of this year’s shortlist. Leading the category is Asake , who pulled off an incredible double entry in the category. He picked up a solo nod for his standout track “ Gratitude ” alongside a stellar collaborative nomination for “ Jogodo ” alongside Wizkid . For Wizkid, this latest nomination adds another major chapter to his historic Grammy legacy, building on his previous career milestones, which include his historic win for Best Music Video with Beyoncé for “ Brown Skin Girl ” at the 63rd Grammy Awards in 2021, as well as multiple past nominations. Tems is another Nigerian nominee, returning to the category she won at the 67th Grammy Awards in February 2025 with “ Love Me JeJe ”. This time, she is nominated for “ Big Daddy ”. Her previous Grammy win came in 2023, when she received Best Melodic Rap Performance for her contribution to Future ‘s “ Wait for U ”, featuring Drake . The Nigerian representation also includes Ayra Starr , whose nomination comes through “ Aye Kan (Are You Coming Back?) ”, a collaboration with Beninese music legend Angélique Kidjo . Ayra Starr previously received a nomination in the category for “ Rush ”, while Angélique Kidjo brings her own Grammy-winning history to the collaboration, with wins for albums including Eve , Sings , Celia and Mother Nature . Rounding out the category with rich cultural resonance are Ghanaian musicians King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni , who earned a brilliant nomination for “ No Tradition, No Africa “. The 69th Grammy Awards will hold on 7 February 2027 at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. The post Asake, Tems, Wizkid & Ayra Starr Lead African Acts Nominated for 2027 Grammys appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Nora Awolowo, Teniola Aladese & Hero Daniels Win Big at The Future Awards Africa 2026 | See Full List
item.description: Nigerian actress, trained lawyer, and TFAA co-host Genoveva Umeh dressed for the 20th edition of The Future Awards Africa. Photo Credit: The Future Awards Africa/Instagram A historic hosting line-up spanning five African countries and the introduction of a first-of-its-kind AI assistant named Infinity marked the 20th edition of The Future Awards Africa (TFAA), held on Saturday, 14 November 2026, at the Balmoral Convention Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. Themed “Celebrating The Redefiners: Africa’s AI Generation,” the ceremony recognised young Africans aged 18 to 35 across 26 categories, including technology and innovation, entrepreneurship, governance, music, film, literature, advocacy, sports and fashion. The anniversary edition was hosted by five personalities from across the continent: Nigerian actress and trained lawyer Genoveva Umeh ; Kenyan media personality Claudia Naisabwa ; Malawian radio broadcaster and television personality Priscilla Kayira ; Botswana television and radio host Resego Motlhokathari ; and Tanzanian actor and former Big Brother Africa winner Idris Sultan . Co-hosts Genoveva Umeh, Resego Motlhokathari, Claudia Naisabwa, Idris Sultan, and Priscilla Kayira pose together ahead of the 20th anniversary ceremony. Photo Credit: The Future Awards Africa/Instagram They shared the stage with Infinity, an AI assistant that interacted with the hosts through quick-witted and playful responses, drawing laughter from guests throughout the ceremony. Its introduction brought artificial intelligence into the evening’s entertainment, while musical performances by Sharp Band and the Loud Urban Choir added to the celebrations. Among the evening’s major winners, Nora Awolowo received the Prize for Young Person of the Year, Teniola Aladese won the Prize for Acting, and Olamidun Ogundoyin took home the Prize for Entrepreneurship. Pastor Jerry Uchechukwu Eze , represented at the ceremony by media personality Hero Daniels , received the Prize for Service to Young People. The ceremony also welcomed representatives of distinguished public figures, including Mobolaji Abubakre Ogunlende , Lagos State Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, who represented Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu . Another highlight was the recognition of the first winners of The Future Awards Africa Independent (TFAAi), a state-level initiative established in 2026 to spotlight young changemakers whose contributions may receive limited attention on national platforms. Its first edition covered Rivers, Abia, Oyo and Kano States, extending the awards’ reach into more communities. Daniel Ekpe (Awkaman) accepts his award on stage at the 20th anniversary edition of The Future Awards Africa. Photo Credit: Daniel Ekpe/Instagram Reflecting on the milestone, Ayodeji Razaq , Executive Director of The Future Awards Africa, said the 20th edition represented a sustained commitment to recognising young Africans shaping the continent’s future. item.title: Familiarity of Doha drives home just how far Socceroos have come in recent years | Joey Lynch
item.description: There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality, highlighted by a return to the scene of Asian Cup heartbreak Last week’s 3-0 dismissal of Qatar at the Abdullah bin Khalifa Stadium marked the first time the Socceroos had returned to the Gulf state since their heartbreaking elimination from the Asian Cup just under three years ago. Back then, coach Graham Arnold called Doha a “home away from home” after they relocated there during the Covid pandemic, and went so far as to suggest that they would have some form of advantage at the 2022 World Cup as a result. Wandering around the city in 2026, memories rush back of Socceroos fans becoming eager participants in the takeover of the city’s souks during the World Cup. So too the feelings of sadness to see the birds still cooped up in small cages at the nearby bird market. It evokes recollections of trips on the red Metro line out to the Al Janoub Stadium in Al Wakrah, aided by the faded posters and stickers celebrating the 2022 tournament’s arrival that to this day can still be seen in shopfronts. There’s the excitement, for some, when a stray cat reminds you just how personable the local felines can be, as well as the sense of unease that remains whenever one pauses to reflect on how all this was built and the hands that did so. Continue reading...

item.title: A long wait, some magic and that smile: Ronaldinho savours Ravenna debut at 46

But on a chilly November day on the eastern coast of Italy, there he was , not only in the squad, but in the starting XI for the eagerly anticipated derby against Forlì as Ravenna chase promotion. item.title: Tiyani Makamu Wins Miss South Africa 2026!
item.description: Tiyani Makamu celebrates on stage moments after being crowned Miss South Africa 2026 at the Sandton Convention Centre in Johannesburg on 14 November 2026. Photo Credit: Miss South Africa/Instagram South Africa has a new queen, and her name is Tiyani Makamu ! At a stylish finale held at the Sandton Convention Centre in Johannesburg on Saturday, 14 November 2026, the 27-year-old entrepreneur and youth advocate from Bronkhorstspruit, Gauteng stepped forward to claim the Miss South Africa 2026 crown. Outgoing titleholder Qhawekazi Mazaleni handed over the reins, while Cwenga Koyana Kotu-Rammopo from Edenvale and Lesego Khumo Nyathela from Springs took home the First Princess and Second Princess titles. Away from the pageant stage, Tiyani Makamu already wears plenty of impressive hats. A graduate of the Pearson Institute of Higher Education, she works as a communications professional, Group Digital Lead, and Client Success Executive, and also runs Hubsela—a small-business support platform she founded to help fellow entrepreneurs build thriving ventures. Her passion for youth employment and business education also shows up in her community work, including supporting a local library initiative in Ivory Park to help young people gain practical skills. Miss South Africa 2026 Tiyani Makamu, entrepreneur and founder of Hubsela from Bronkhorstspruit, Gauteng. Photo Credit: Miss South Africa/Instagram What makes Tiyani Makamu’s reign especially exciting is how different Miss South Africa 2026 looks this year. Under the Motsepe Group of Companies’ ownership, the Miss South Africa Organisation shifted its focus toward homegrown leadership and social impact—meaning neither Makamu nor her runners-up will head off to international competitions like Miss Universe, Miss World, or Miss Supranational. Instead, she gets to pour her entire year into community projects across South Africa through the pageant’s Empower Youth Africa initiative, backed by a R1 million cash prize and access to up to R500,000 from the Impact Fund. Chatting shortly after her crowning at the Sandton Convention Centre—which hosted the finale for the first time after four years in Pretoria—Miss South Africa 2026 Tiyani Makamu shared what she hopes to accomplish over the next twelve months: My mandate as Miss South Africa is to empower women entrepreneurs by bridging the gaps in access to opportunities, business development and funding. I want to equip women with the skills, resources and financial readiness to build sustainable, thriving businesses. Through entrepreneurship and skills development, I aim to champion the economic empowerme nt of women and youth across Afr ica. Miss South Africa 2026 Tiyani Makamu, who will dedicate her reign to domestic entrepreneurship and youth empowerment across South Africa. Photo Credit: Tiyani Makamu/Instagram The post Tiyani Makamu Wins Miss South Africa 2026! appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .
